docs.title: How this site is organised
docs.text: Path What lives there projects/<name>/ A self-contained three.js app (index.html, styles.css, src/) docs/ This MkDocs Material site scripts/build-site.sh Builds the docs and copies every app to site/apps/<name>/ .github/workflows/deploy.yml Builds on every push and publishes main to the gh-pages branch

docs.title: Contributing a project
docs.text: Each visualisation is a standalone folder under projects/ plus a docs section.

docs.title: 1. Create the app folder
docs.text:
projects/<your-project>/
├── index.html      # import map + UI shell
├── styles.css
├── README.md       # short summary (not published)
└── src/
    └── main.js

Start the index.html with an import map pinned to an exact three.js version:

<script type="importmap">
  {
    "imports": {
      "three": "https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/three@0.170.0/build/three.module.js",
      "three/addons/": "https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/three@0.170.0/examples/jsm/"
    }
  }
</script>
<script type="module" src="./src/main.js"></script>

Keep paths relative (./src/…). The app is published at /apps/<your-project>/.

docs.title: 2. Add documentation
docs.text:
1. Create docs/projects/<your-project>/index.md and link to the app with ../../apps/<your-project>/.
  2. Add the pages to nav: in mkdocs.yml.
  3. Add a row to docs/projects/index.md and a card to docs/index.md.
  4. Put screenshots in docs/assets/<your-project>/ (JPEG, ~1600 px wide).

docs.title: 3. Preview
docs.text:
pip install -r requirements.txt
scripts/build-site.sh --serve      # docs + apps on http://localhost:8000
# or, docs only with live reload:
mkdocs serve

docs.title: 4. Publish
docs.text:
Pushing to main runs .github/workflows/deploy.yml. It checks JavaScript syntax, builds the docs with --strict, bundles every app and force-pushes the result to the gh-pages branch.

One-time GitHub setup

In Settings → Pages, set Source to Deploy from a branch, branch gh-pages, folder / (root). The site is then served at https://<user>.github.io/3D-Artifacts/.

docs.title: Guidelines
docs.text:
• Use real units and published dimensions. Cite the sources on the project's reference page.
  • Keep data (src/data/) separate from rendering code.
  • Make the UI work at phone width, and give every view a keyboard shortcut.
  • Prefer procedural textures. Load large imagery from a pinned CDN URL with a fallback.

docs.title: Shared conventions
docs.text:
• No build step. Apps are plain ES modules. three is loaded from jsDelivr via an import map pinned to an exact version, so the folder can be served by any static host.
  • Real units. Scenes use metres (or the natural SI unit of the subject) so that published dimensions can be typed in directly.
  • Data separate from code. Specifications and scripted sequences live in src/data/, so they can be checked against sources without reading render code.
  • Modern UI. Glass panels, a transport bar, keyboard shortcuts, deep-linkable state (?mission=…&t=…&view=…), and responsive down to phone width.

docs.title: AI Factory India: Vera Rubin NVL72
docs.text:
A 3D walkthrough of an illustrative 100 MW AI factory near Hyderabad, built on NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 racks. It zooms in eight steps, from the 220 kV grid and the dry-cooler yard down to a single Rubin GPU package. The Indian sun, Hyderabad's climate and the workload all change the readouts live.

Launch the walkthrough Source on GitHub

What is real and what is illustrative

Rack, superchip, GPU and 100 MW factory figures come from NVIDIA's public Vera Rubin NVL72 page, and the tray layout comes from NVIDIA's DGX documentation. The site itself, including its layout, solar field, cooling setpoints, per-rack power and plant model, is an illustrative design, not a real facility. This is an independent visualisation, not affiliated with NVIDIA.

docs.title: The eight stops
docs.text: # Stop What you see 1 The AI factory 100 MW campus: 4 halls × 139 racks = 556 NVL72 ≈ 40,000 Rubin GPUs 2 Power in 220 kV line → 220/33 kV substation → 33 kV feeders to each hall; 4.9 MWp solar field; 24 diesel generators 3 Warm-water cooling Pipe rack and 64 dry coolers; fans speed up with the heat; adiabatic mist on the hottest hours 4 Data hall Cutaway: 8 rows of racks, in-row CDUs, overhead pipes, busways, fibre trays, plus power, cooling, network and UPS rooms 5 Vera Rubin NVL72 18 compute trays, 9 NVLink 6 switch trays, power shelves, management switches 6 Compute tray The tray slides out, the lid lifts and the cold plates rise to show 4 Rubin GPUs, 2 Vera CPUs, ConnectX-9 and BlueField-4 7 NVLink 6 spine Rear of the rack: copper cable cartridges carrying data pulses, coolant manifolds and the DC busbar 8 Tokens out Requests and tokens streaming between the site and 14 Indian cities, at 3 m per km

docs.title: Data hall
docs.text: 139 racks fit in about 17 m × 24 m of white space. The rooms that power and cool them take most of the building.

docs.title: One NVL72 rack
docs.text: 72 Rubin GPUs and 36 Vera CPUs acting as one accelerator: 3,600 PFLOPS NVFP4 inference and 20.7 TB HBM4.

docs.title: Compute tray, exploded
docs.text: Each Rubin package: 2 compute dies, 2 I/O dies, 8 HBM4 stacks (12 chips, 288 GB). Hoses run supply → GPU → GPU → CPU → return for each superchip.

docs.title: NVLink 6 spine
docs.text: Copper cartridges link every GPU to all nine switch trays: 3 TB/s per GPU, 216 TB/s per rack.

docs.title: 15 May, 15:00 IST, 39 °C
docs.text: The dry coolers can't reach a 42 °C supply on their own, so adiabatic assist switches on and uses about 5 m³/h of water.

docs.title: Tokens to India
docs.text: Distances and one-way fibre latency (route ≈ 1.4 × straight line, 200 km/ms in glass).

docs.title: Why India changes the design
docs.text:
• Heat. Hyderabad's May afternoons reach about 39–40 °C. Vera Rubin accepts coolant up to 45 °C, so a 42 °C supply is possible with dry coolers alone whenever it is below about 37 °C outside. Most of the year needs no chillers and no water. Try Summer peak versus Winter.
  • Monsoon. June to September brings cloud and afternoon rain. On-site solar drops by about two thirds, while the cooling plant runs easily.
  • Green power. On-site solar covers only a few percent of 100 MW. Indian data centres buy most green energy through open-access solar and wind contracts wheeled over the grid.
  • Demand. Inference follows Indian daily life, with a morning peak and a larger evening peak around 21:00 IST. Training runs flat out.

Real projects in the same space include AM Intelligence's Vera Rubin NVL72 order for a 30 MW AI factory in Hyderabad, slated for Q1 2027, and gigawatt-scale plans from L&T, Reliance and Yotta.

docs.text: Stops Top bar, ← →, or Tour (T) for a guided loop Clock Live IST by default; drag the slider for any hour; 1× … 1 h/s; Space pauses Season Today, Summer peak (15 May), Monsoon (20 Jul), Winter (15 Dec) Workload Inference (daily demand curve) or Training (94 % flat) Toggles Flows (power, coolant, data), Labels, Cutaway (Hall A roof) Deep links #/tray?season=summer&hour=15&mode=training

docs.title: The plant model
docs.text:
src/sim/env.js is deliberately simple and easy to check:

  • Sun: a low-precision solar ephemeris for 17.385° N, 78.487° E, plus the three.js Sky.
  • Ambient: monthly Hyderabad normals, with the minimum at 06:00 and the maximum at 15:00.
  • IT load: 88 MW × (0.30 + 0.70 × utilisation). The 88 MW IT share of the 100 MW envelope is assumed.
  • Coolant: constant flow sized for ΔT = 10 K at full load, with return = supply + 10 K × load.
  • Adiabatic water: the evaporated share of heat ÷ 2.45 MJ/kg.
  • PUE: 1 + electrical losses (3.5 %) + misc (1 %) + pumps (1.2 %) + fans (0.6–2.8 %, rising with ambient temperature).
  • NVFP4 compute in use: utilisation × 2 ZFLOPS for inference, or × 1.4 ZFLOPS for training.

docs.title: Cloud Brick Architect
docs.text:
A 2D brick-building game for cloud architecture. AWS services are bricks with studs, and the Region, VPC, Availability Zone and subnet groups are baseplates that carry the bricks inside them. Snap bricks onto the board and connect them. Each mission checks your design live, so you can then run traffic through it and knock out an Availability Zone to see if it survives.

Play Source on GitHub

docs.title: Missions
docs.text:
# Mission You learn Budget 1 Static website S3 origin behind CloudFront; Route 53, ACM and WAF as bonuses $20 2 Serverless API API Gateway → Lambda → DynamoDB; Cognito auth, CloudWatch, X-Ray $50 3 Highly available web app VPC, 2 AZs, private subnets, ALB, EC2, RDS Multi-AZ; must survive an AZ failure $300 4 Event-driven photo tagging S3 events → SQS → Lambda → Rekognition → DynamoDB; DLQ and SNS $60 5 Clickstream data lake Kinesis → Firehose → S3, Glue catalogue, Athena; Lake Formation, Glacier, KMS $120 6 GenAI assistant (RAG) API Gateway → Lambda → Bedrock, S3 knowledge base, OpenSearch vectors $400 ∞ Sandbox Free build —

Stars:

  • ★ for meeting all the goals.
  • ★★ for meeting them within the budget.
  • ★★★ for also completing every bonus.

Your best stars and each mission's board are saved in your browser.

docs.text: Six missions from beginner to advanced, plus a sandbox.

docs.title: Run traffic
docs.text: Requests flow as animated packets from Users. Bricks off the request path, such as WAF, Cognito and the S3 ingestion side, are dimmed.

docs.title: Mission complete
docs.text: Stars, confetti and a one-line lesson for each mission.

docs.title: How to play
docs.text: Action How Add a service or group Drag it from the palette onto the board, or click it to drop it in the centre Move Drag a brick. Drag a group by its label to move it with everything on it Resize a group Drag its bottom-right corner Connect Drag from the orange ● on a brick's right edge to another brick, or use Connect mode (C): tap one brick, then another Select / delete Click a brick or arrow, then press Delete. Selected arrows can be reversed Pan / zoom Drag empty board or right-drag · mouse wheel or pinch · F fits the view Undo / redo Ctrl+Z / Ctrl+Y · Ctrl+D duplicates a brick Run traffic R or Run traffic Chaos test Fail an AZ takes each Availability Zone offline in turn Hint Highlights the bricks the next goal needs Export PNG diagram, JSON (re-importable)

docs.title: How a design is checked
docs.text:
src/graph.js turns the board into a graph:

  • Containment: a brick belongs to every group its centre sits in. This gives questions like "is every EC2 in a private subnet?" and "are the EC2 instances spread over two AZs?".
  • Connections: arrows are directed edges, so a check can ask for a direct edge (edge(a, b)), an edge either way (linked) or a reachable path (path).
  • AZ failure: survivesAZ(a, b) removes every brick inside one AZ at a time and checks that a path from a to b still exists.
    • This is why mission 3 needs a load balancer that spans both AZs, which means placing it in the VPC outside the AZ plates.
    • It also needs a standby database in the second AZ.

Each mission goal is a one-line test on that graph, so new missions are easy to add in src/levels.js.

docs.title: Brick Builder
docs.text:
A 3D builder for interlocking plastic bricks with the classic dimensions. Pick a part and a colour, then click to snap it onto the studs. Parts stack, rotate, repaint and undo. Replay a build brick by brick, export it as a file, or save a screenshot.

Launch the builder Source on GitHub

docs.title: Real dimensions
docs.text:
Every part is modelled in millimetres:

Stud pitch 8.0 mm Plate height 3.2 mm Brick height 9.6 mm (3 plates) Stud Ø 4.8 mm × 1.7 mm Clearance 0.1 mm on every side, so neighbouring bricks show a hairline seam Baseplate 16, 32 or 48 studs (12.8, 25.6 or 38.4 cm)

docs.title: Parts and colours
docs.text:
• 34 parts:
    • Bricks: 1×1 to 2×8.
    • Plates: 1×1 to 6×8.
    • Tiles: smooth, with no studs.
    • 45° slopes: 2×1 to 2×4.
    • Round: round brick, round plate and cone.
  • 24 classic colours, including transparent ones, using the hex values from the Rebrickable colour catalogue.

docs.title: How building works
docs.text:
• Snapping: the ghost part follows the cursor and snaps to the stud grid. Point at the top of a part to stack on it, or at its side to place next to it.
  • Gravity: a new part drops onto the highest stud under its footprint, so it can overhang but never float.
  • Real connections only: you can't press a part onto a smooth tile or the sloped face of a slope. The ghost turns red when a spot isn't allowed.
  • Rotation: R turns the part a quarter turn. Slopes rotate in all four directions.

docs.title: Building
docs.text: Bricks stacking and overhanging, with a red ghost where a brick won't fit on a tile.

docs.title: Rainbow tower
docs.text: 27 crossed 2×4 bricks in a spiral, 26.9 cm tall.

docs.title: Heart mosaic
docs.text: 256 1×1 tiles on 4×4 plates, drawn from the heart curve (x² + y² − 1)³ − x²y³ ≤ 0.

docs.title: Controls
docs.text: Action Mouse / touch Keys Place part Click / tap Orbit · pan · zoom Drag · right-drag · wheel / pinch F frames the build Rotate part Rotate button R (Shift+R back) Tools Build · Paint · Erase · Pick B P E I Quick erase / pick Shift-click / Alt-click Delete erases the hovered part Colour Palette [ ] Undo / redo Arrow buttons Ctrl+Z / Ctrl+Y

docs.title: Saving
docs.text:
• Auto-save: the build is saved in your browser and comes back on your next visit.
  • Export / import: writes and reads a small JSON file. Each part is stored as [partId, colour, x, y, z, rotation], so builds are easy to share or generate in code:
{ "v": 1, "base": 32, "baseColor": 9,
  "bricks": [["brick-4x2", 4, 14, 0, 15, 0], ["slope-2x2", 5, 14, 3, 15, 2]] }
  • Screenshot: saves a PNG of the current view, without the ghost part.
  • Replay: rebuilds the model from the bottom up, brick by brick.

docs.title: Brick Studio Pro
docs.text:
An advanced 3D builder for interlocking plastic bricks, a step up from Brick Builder. Parts snap only where their studs and anti-studs actually connect. You can select and edit groups of parts, check whether a build would hold together, and get building instructions and a parts list. Generators make shapes, lettering and photo mosaics, and builds export to LDraw and BrickLink.

Open Brick Studio Pro Source on GitHub

Note

Brick Studio is an independent project, not affiliated with or endorsed by the LEGO Group. Part and colour numbers are given for convenience; check them before ordering. Weights and prices are estimates.

docs.title: Parts and colours
docs.text:
There are 69 parts in seven categories and 40 colours, including transparent ones.

Category Parts Bricks 1×1 to 2×8, a 2×2 corner and a 1×2 grille Plates 1×1 to 8×8, a 2×2 corner, left and right wedge plates and a 1×2 jumper Tiles 1×1 to 2×4 and a round 1×1 tile Slopes 45°, 33° and 65° slopes, inverted slopes and curved slopes Round Round 1×1 and 2×2 bricks and plates, a cone and a dome Arches & windows Arches, window frames, a door frame and a fence Technic Technic bricks 1×2 to 1×8 with pin holes

Each part carries its LDraw / BrickLink part number, and each colour its LDraw and BrickLink colour numbers. Search the parts panel by name or number.

Units follow the real system: one stud is 8 mm, a plate is 3.2 mm and a brick is three plates.

docs.title: Building
docs.text:
Tool Key What it does Build B Place the current part. R rotates it Select S Click, shift-click or drag a box to select parts Paint P Recolour a part with the current colour Erase E Remove a part (or shift-click with any tool) Pick I Take the part and colour from the build (or alt-click)

Snapping. A part goes where it really connects:

  • on top of studs;
  • under an overhang, held by the anti-studs of the part above;
  • beside a part, dropped to the nearest connecting height.

Tiles and slope faces have no studs, so nothing attaches on top of them. Free placement lifts the connection rule; PgUp / PgDn then lift the part.

Editing a selection.

  • Move with the arrow keys and PgUp / PgDn; rotate with R; mirror with M.
  • Ctrl+C / Ctrl+V copy and paste on top; Ctrl+D duplicates beside.
  • The inspector lists what is selected and has buttons to rotate, mirror, duplicate, copy, paint, delete or deselect it. Ctrl+A selects everything.
  • Replace a colour everywhere swaps one colour for another across the build.
  • Undo and redo cover every change.

docs.title: Checking a build
docs.text:
The Check tab analyses the connections between parts:

  • Floating parts are not connected to the baseplate through any chain of studs. They show in red.
  • Weak joints hang on a single stud. They show in amber.
  • It reports the number of separate groups, the weight, the height and the centre of mass.
  • Drop test animates what would happen if you lifted the model: unsupported groups fall.

docs.title: Building instructions

docs.title: CAD/CAM Studio
docs.text:
A browser CAD/CAM workbench in three.js:

  • Design: model a machined part from parametric features, with true solid booleans.
  • Manufacture: switch to this workspace to get toolpaths automatically.
  • Simulate: watch the cutter remove material, and check the result against the design.
  • Export: GRBL G-code, an STL of the part, or the project file.

Open the studio Source on GitHub

docs.title: Design (CAD)
docs.text:
The part is a stock block minus machining features, rebuilt as a solid by constructive solid geometry (three-bvh-csg) every time a value changes.

Feature Parameters Facing depth Rectangular pocket centre, width, length, corner radius, depth Circular pocket centre, diameter, depth Slot centre, overall length, width, angle, depth Holes diameter, depth or through; single, grid (count and pitch) or bolt circle (count, radius, start angle). Blind holes get a 118° drill point Outside profile rectangle (with corner radius) or circle; through or to depth

The studio works the way a CAD program does:

  • Selecting: click a face in the viewport to select its feature.
  • Editing: every value is live-editable, and features can be duplicated, suppressed or deleted.
  • Undo: undo/redo with Ctrl+Z / Ctrl+Y.
  • Part data: the panel shows part volume, mass for the chosen material and the percentage of material removed.
  • Materials: aluminium 6061, brass, acrylic, HDPE, oak and MDF.

docs.title: Manufacture (CAM)
docs.text:
Each feature gets an operation with a sensible tool from the library, and every setting can be edited.

Operation Strategy Face Zig-zag rows across the stock with a face mill, entering from outside the material Pocket Offset: concentric offsets cut from the centre outwards, with a helical entry and climb milling. Zig-zag (rectangles): raster rows with a ramp entry plus a finishing pass Slot Ramped centre-line passes when the tool matches the slot width, otherwise a pocket Drill Peck drilling in the style of G83, written out as G0/G1 moves Helical bore For holes with no matching drill: a helix at the hole radius minus the tool radius, then a clean-up circle Profile Outside contour, climb milled, with a ramp entry on every level. Holding tabs keep the part attached on the last passes

How the toolpaths are computed:

  • Offsets: the shapes are convex (rounded rectangle, circle, slot), so offsets are exact and analytic: no polygon-clipping approximations.
  • Pocket centres: a medial "spine" pass clears the middle of long pockets.
  • Feeds and speeds: calculated from the material's cutting speed (Vc) and a chip load that scales with tool diameter: rpm = Vc·1000 / (π·D) (capped by the machine), feed = rpm · flutes · fz.
  • Overrides: spindle speed, feed, stepdown, stepover and peck depth can each be overridden per operation.
  • Warnings: the studio flags problems such as a tool too large for a pocket, a drill that doesn't match its hole, a depth beyond the flute length, or corners that will keep the tool's radius.

docs.title: Toolpaths
docs.text: Cuts are drawn in each operation's colour, plunges in yellow and rapids as dashed red lines.

docs.title: Simulation + live G-code
docs.text: The spindle, holder and cutter follow the program while chips fly. The current G-code line is highlighted.

docs.title: Compare with the design
docs.text: Green is on size, amber is stock left (here the four holding tabs), red would be a gouge, and brown is scrap outside the profile.

docs.title: Material-removal simulation
docs.text:
The stock is a height field ("Z-map") with a cell size of about 0.3 mm.

  • Cutting: every feed move sweeps the tool along the segment. Each cell within the tool radius is lowered to the tool's underside: flat, ball, 118° drill point or face mill.
  • Scrubbing: you can scrub the timeline anywhere; going backwards replays the program from the start in milliseconds.
  • Checking: Compare colours each cell against the designed surface. On both samples, 99.7% of cells are on size. The only stock left is the holding tabs, and "gouges" are a handful of single cells on edges, from grid sampling.

docs.title: Output
docs.text:
Export Contents G-code (.nc) GRBL-flavoured: G21 G90 G94 G17 G54, T# M6, S… M3, G0/G1 only (canned cycles expanded), ASCII comments STL Binary, millimetres, Z up, straight from the CSG solid Project (.json) Stock, machine, features, tools and operations, which can be reopened later

The work origin (G54 X0 Y0 Z0) is the top surface at the front-left corner of the stock. The project also autosaves in the browser.

docs.title: Samples
docs.text:
• Motor mounting plate (aluminium 6061, 120 × 80 × 12): facing, a 64 × 40 R6 pocket, a Ø22 bearing bore, 6 × M5 tapping holes on a bolt circle, 4 × Ø6.6 clearance holes (helically bored), a cable slot and a through profile with 4 tabs. Cycle time is about 9 minutes with 5 tools.
  • Oak coaster (100 × 100 × 10): a Ø80 cup recess, a centre dimple, two crossed grooves and a Ø94 round profile.

Not for real machining without review

This is an educational CAM. It does no collision checking for holders, has no adaptive clearing, and does not check fixtures. Always verify G-code in your own simulator and air-cut before running a real machine.

docs.title: CRS-35: Launch to Docking
docs.text:
A 3D animation of NASA's 35th SpaceX Commercial Resupply mission (Oct 2026), from the pre-dawn countdown at Cape Canaveral to Cargo Dragon docking with the International Space Station 51 hours later.

Launch the animation Source on GitHub

docs.title: The mission
docs.text: Liftoff 13 Oct 2026, 6:33 a.m. EDT, Falcon 9 from SLC-40, Cape Canaveral Space Force Station Dragon separation About 9 minutes after launch, followed by nosecone opening and phasing burns Docking ≈ 11:00 a.m. EDT, 15 Oct 2026, on Harmony's space-facing (zenith) port Cargo More than 6,300 lb of science and supplies, including the final pair of iROSAs Hardware Booster on its 8th flight, Dragon on its 4th Stay About one month, then splashdown in the Pacific

docs.title: Three acts on one clock
docs.text: The animation runs on Mission Elapsed Time (MET). Each act has its own scene, cameras and readouts, plus a fixed share of the scrubber so the 10-minute launch isn't lost in the 51-hour total.

docs.title: 1 · Launch & landing (T−1:30 → T+13 min)
docs.text: Countdown, liftoff, Max-Q, MECO, stage separation, second-stage burn. The booster does its boostback, entry and landing burns back to a Cape landing zone. Then SECO, Dragon separation and nosecone opening.

docs.title: Booster return
docs.text: Grid fins deploy, the booster flips for boostback, coasts to apogee and falls back engines-first. Legs deploy for the landing burn.

docs.title: 2 · Orbit phasing (≈ 51 h)
docs.text: The globe shows the station's and Dragon's orbits over a rotating Earth. Burns raise Dragon from ≈ 210 km while it catches up with the ISS, which starts about 277° ahead.

docs.title: 3 · Rendezvous & docking
docs.text: Approach ellipsoid, Waypoint 0, Keep-Out Sphere fly-around, Waypoints 1 and 2, then autonomous final approach to IDA-3 on Harmony and soft and hard capture.

docs.title: What is modelled, and how
docs.text:
Part Approach Vehicles Falcon 9 Block 5 at published size (3.7 m wide, ≈ 69 m tall with Dragon): nine Merlins, interstage, grid fins, landing legs, MVac. Cargo Dragon has a trunk carrying the iROSA pair and a hinged nosecone. Pad & landing zone SLC-40 with crew access tower, transporter-erector, lightning masts and floodlights. A landing zone about 9 km south. Launch frame A local frame at the pad's real coordinates, aimed along the ≈ 45° launch azimuth for a 51.64° orbit. The textured Earth is positioned so Florida's coast lies under the pad. Lighting The Sun's real position at 6:33 a.m. EDT is 11.5° below the horizon. The pad is dark, but each exhaust puff is tested against Earth's shadow, so the plume lights up as it climbs into sunlight (the twilight effect seen across the south-east US). Ascent A smooth reconstruction of a typical Falcon 9 ISS profile: MECO ≈ T+2:18, SECO ≈ T+8:35, Dragon separation at T+9:00. Orbit plane The ISS plane passes through SLC-40 at liftoff (an instantaneous launch window), computed from the pad latitude, longitude and sidereal time. Phasing Dragon flies a series of burns from ≈ 210 km up to the ISS altitude. The ISS phase is solved so the two meet at the docking time. Rendezvous The same LVLH approach as the station project, with the station from the ISS project configured for 15 Oct 2026.

Illustrative parts

NASA publishes the key times but not the trajectory. Altitudes, speeds, burn times, the landing-zone position and the phasing burn plan are representative of Falcon 9 / Dragon flights, not CRS-35 telemetry. The booster landing shown is the planned return-to-launch-site recovery; I found no post-launch confirmation.

docs.title: Krishi Yantra · Farm tractors
docs.text:
Farm tractors and their implements, animated in 3D. Hitch an implement, watch it work a field, and follow a whole wheat season: ploughing paddy stubble in October to taking the grain to the mandi in April.

Open Krishi Yantra Source on GitHub

Note

The tractors and implements are generic, with no brands. Figures (widths, speeds, field capacity, fuel, prices) are illustrative rules of thumb from Indian farm practice. Makers' manuals and local agricultural university advice govern.

docs.title: Tractors
docs.text:
Tractor Power Drive Weight Lift Indicative price 35 HP 26 kW 2WD, ROPS canopy 1,800 kg 1,200 kg ₹5.5–6.5 lakh 50 HP 37 kW 2WD, ROPS canopy 2,100 kg 1,800 kg ₹7.5–8.8 lakh 75 HP 55 kW 4WD, closed cab 3,200 kg 2,500 kg ₹12.5–15 lakh

docs.title: Earthmovers
docs.text:
A 3D portfolio of heavy construction equipment. Eight machine classes, each a working model you can:

  • inspect in a showroom;
  • operate joint by joint;
  • configure and price;
  • compare with the others;
  • plan a fleet around;
  • dig with in a sandbox;
  • watch on a busy job site.

Open Earthmovers Source on GitHub

Note

The machines are generic and modelled on typical machines of each class. They carry no manufacturer's branding. Specifications and prices are illustrative class values, not any manufacturer's published figures. Earthmovers is not affiliated with any equipment maker.

docs.title: The machines
docs.text:
Machine Class Typical work Class examples Backhoe loader ≈8 t · 55 kW Trenching, utilities, loading JCB 3DX / 3CX, CAT 424 / 432 Hydraulic excavator ≈20 t · 110 kW Mass excavation, truck loading CAT 320, JCB JS205 Wheel loader ≈19 t · 140 kW, 3.1 m³ Stockpiles, truck and hopper loading CAT 950, JCB 456 Crawler dozer ≈20 t · 160 kW Pushing, spreading, ripping CAT D6 Rigid haul truck 90 t payload · 760 kW Open-pit mines and quarries CAT 777 Motor grader ≈16 t · 140 kW, 3.7 m blade Roads, fine grading CAT 140 Telescopic handler 3.5 t · 9.5 m Lifting materials on building sites JCB 535-95, CAT TH357 Skid steer loader ≈3 t · 900 kg ROC Small sites, cleaning, landscaping JCB Robot, CAT 226

Each machine is built in code, with no model files:

  • extruded booms, sticks and loader arms;
  • crawler tracks whose shoes run round the sprocket and idler;
  • lugged tyres;
  • cabs with an operator;
  • lamps and beacons.

Hydraulic rams. These connect the parts the way real cylinders do. Each ram is pinned at both ends, so when a joint moves, the rod slides in or out of the barrel.

docs.title: Showroom
docs.text:
• Turntable and cameras: 3/4, side, front, top and a cab view from the operator's seat.
  • Hotspots: click one to fly to the cab, engine, boom, tracks, counterweight and more, with a short note on each.
  • Dimensions: overall length, width and height of the current pose.
  • Working range: a reach chart computed from the model's own linkage.
    • The app sweeps the boom, stick or dipper (and telescope) through their ranges and plots every tool-tip position.
    • It reports the maximum height, reach at ground level and dig depth.
  • Overview tab: a typical specification sheet, applications and an indicative price range.

docs.title: Operate
docs.text:
Every joint has a slider and two keys:

Machine Joints Excavator Swing, boom, stick, bucket. Keys follow the ISO joystick pattern: A/D swing, W/S stick, I/K boom, J/L bucket Backhoe loader Backhoe swing, boom, dipper, extending dipper, bucket; loader arms and bucket; stabilisers Wheel loader Articulation, Z-bar lift arms, bucket tilt Crawler dozer Blade lift, pitch and tilt; ripper Haul truck Body raise Motor grader Circle angle, blade lift, side shift Telehandler Boom angle, three-section telescope, carriage tilt with automatic fork levelling, stabilisers Skid steer Lift arms, tilt

Demo cycle plays a typical work cycle for each machine. The tool-tip panel shows reach, height and height above the ground live.

Attachments change the tool on the end of the arm: - excavator: general-purpose, rock and ditching buckets, a breaker; - backhoe: buckets, a breaker, an auger; - wheel loader: buckets and forks; - telehandler: forks, a bucket, a jib; - skid steer: a bucket, forks, an auger, a sweeper.

docs.title: Configure and price
docs.text:
• Fleet livery in seven colours.
  • Attachment and options:
    • LED work lights, which visibly light up, and a rotating beacon;
    • an air-conditioned cab and telematics;
    • cameras and fire suppression;
    • grade control, payload weighing and an extended warranty.
  • Quote: base price, attachment, options, GST at 18% and an on-road estimate.
  • Finance: down payment, interest rate and tenure give the EMI. An owning-and-operating cost per hour is also shown.
  • Download the quote as a text file.

docs.title: Compare
docs.text: Bar charts compare operating weight, engine power, indicative price, fuel tank, top speed and power-to-weight. A side-by-side table follows. Click a bar to open that machine.

docs.title: Fleet planner
docs.text:
Plan a cut-and-haul job. Pick:

  • a loading machine (excavator, wheel loader, backhoe or skid steer) with its current bucket;
  • a material: common earth, wet clay, sand and gravel, or blasted rock;
  • a hauler: a 16 m³ road tipper, a 30 t articulated dump truck or the 90 t haul truck;
  • the haul distance, job volume and hours per day.

The planner works out:

  • passes per load: the bucket's loose volume after its fill factor, limited by the hauler's volume or payload;
  • the hauler cycle: spot, load, haul loaded, dump, return, shown as a timeline;
  • the haulers needed to keep the loader busy;
  • production in bank m³/h, with a 50-minute working hour and the material's swell;
  • days for the job, cost per bank m³ from owning-and-operating rates, and fleet fuel with its CO₂.

It warns when the pass count falls outside the usual 3–6, which means the loader and hauler are mismatched.

docs.title: Sandbox
docs.text:
Drive any machine on a 56 m × 56 m deformable ground. Use ↑/↓ to drive and ←/→ to steer: - tracked machines counter-rotate their tracks; - the wheel loader articulates; - the others steer their wheels.

The ground is a heightfield with a 0.25 m grid.

  • Buckets cut the ground wherever their teeth go below it and carry the soil, which shows in the bucket.
    • When the bucket's opening turns downward, the soil pours out.
    • Over the dump truck it fills the body. Anywhere else it piles up and slumps to a 38° angle of repose.
  • Blades:
    • The dozer pushes a growing pile ahead of its blade.
    • The grader rolls a windrow off the trailing end of its moldboard.
    • A blade cuts at most 0.3 m below the tracks, so a dozer cannot bury itself.
  • The auger drills a hole.
  • The HUD shows the bucket load, the dump truck's payload, the volume dug and the speed. Reset ground restores the terrain.

The dump truck here is the haul truck at 65% scale (≈16 m³, ≈26–30 t). That size suits a 20 t excavator: a 90 t truck is loaded by excavators of 70 t or more.

docs.title: Job site
docs.text:
All eight machines work at once on looping cycles:

  • Excavator and dump trucks: the excavator digs at a face and loads two dump trucks in turn, four passes each. Between trucks it trims the face.
  • Haul road: the trucks drive a loop to a dump, tip their bodies, and return.
  • Dozer: spreads the dump pile.
  • Wheel loader: works a V-pattern between an aggregate stockpile and a crusher feed hopper.
  • Motor grader: trims the access road with its blade angled, then backs up.
  • Backhoe loader: digs a trench, with its stabilisers down.
  • Telehandler: lifts pallets of blocks onto the first floor of a building under construction.
  • Skid steer: cleans up and stockpiles spoil.

Counters track the shift clock, truck loads, tonnes hauled, crusher feed, pallets lifted, trench dug and fleet fuel. Run time at 1×, 4× or 12×, or pause it. Click any machine's label to follow it with the camera.

The rams are calibrated when a machine is built. The app sweeps the joints each ram depends on to find its shortest and longest pin-to-pin distance, then sizes the barrel and rod so the rod never leaves the barrel.

docs.title: ISS EVA Spacewalk
docs.text:
A real-time 3D simulation of spacewalks (Extravehicular Activities, EVAs) on the International Space Station, built with three.js.

Launch the simulator Source on GitHub

docs.title: What is real
docs.text:
Aspect How it is modelled Station geometry Every pressurised module, the 109 m Integrated Truss Structure (S0–S6, P1–P6), 8 Solar Array Wings (35 m × 12 m), iROSAs, radiators, Canadarm2, Dextre and visiting vehicles, sized to published figures. See the station reference. Configuration by date Each mission shows the station as it was on that date: Pirs before July 2021, Nauka and Prichal after, Bishop from December 2020, iROSAs added in 2021–2023. Orbit Circular orbit at 415 km and 51.64° inclination, Keplerian period (92.7 min), speed 7.66 km/s, live latitude/longitude ground track. Sun & Earth Solar position from the date (Astronomical Almanac low-precision formula), Earth rotated by Greenwich sidereal time. Day/night, the beta angle, sunrise/sunset countdowns and the city lights below all follow from those two. Power & thermal In free orbit the SARJs and Beta Gimbals point every wing at the Sun, and the radiators turn edge-on to it. During EVAs the arrays are parked and locked. EVA procedures Hatch → safety tether → translation → worksite → robotic arm hand-offs → ingress, with task order and durations based on real spacewalks. Suits NASA EMU (EV1 has red stripes) and Roscosmos Orlan-MKS (red / blue stripes), with PLSS, SAFER, helmet lights and gold visors.

What is illustrative

Crew routes are plausible paths along real structure, not surveyed handrail positions. Suit telemetry (O₂, CO₂, battery, heart rate) is simulated for display. The orbit is circular and ignores drag and Earth's oblateness (J2).

docs.title: Two-pass rendering
docs.text:
The Earth is 6,786 km from the station's centre, but the camera can sit 5 cm from a helmet. One depth buffer cannot cover both ranges, so each frame is drawn twice through an EffectComposer:

  1. Far pass: Earth, atmosphere, stars and the Sun, with a camera whose near/far planes are 20 km / 120,000 km.
  2. Near pass: the station and crew, with near/far 5 cm / 4 km. The depth buffer is cleared first and the colour buffer is kept.
  3. Bloom and output: an Unreal bloom pass for the Sun and specular glints, then ACES tone mapping.

Both cameras share position and orientation, so the two layers line up exactly.

docs.title: Orbit & lighting
docs.text:
Orbit.state(t) returns everything the frame needs:

  • Position: ECI position and velocity directions of a circular orbit, Rz(Ω)·Rx(i)·[cos u, sin u, 0].
  • Station frame (LVLH): x = velocity, y = radial, z = x × y (starboard).
  • Sun: solar longitude from the date, projected into the station frame.
  • Beta angle and eclipse: β = asin(ŝ · ĥ). The Sun is eclipsed when its angle from nadir is less than Earth's angular radius, asin(R⊕ / r) ≈ 69.7°, which also gives analytic sunrise and sunset countdowns.
  • Earth orientation: M = L · Rz(GMST) · P turns the textured sphere so the real coastline sits under the station.

Sunlight fades over about 1.5° around the limb with a warm tint, so orbital sunsets look as fast as they are in reality (about 10 seconds at 1×).

docs.title: Mission timeline
docs.text:
MissionPlayer compiles a mission (authored in minutes) into tracks:

  • Vector tracks (crew, arm end-effectors, payloads) use eased interpolation between keys. The segment direction drives head-first translation and the hand-over-hand limb cycle.
  • Scalar tracks drive the MBS rail position, hatch angle, iROSA visibility and roll-out fraction.
  • Attachments make one track follow another (ev2 on arm, battery on ev1). At compile time the player inserts keys at each attachment boundary, so pick-ups and hand-offs are continuous.
  • Live carriers: at run time, attached objects follow the solved arm tip rather than the requested one. If a target is out of reach, the astronaut stays on the foot restraint instead of floating free.

docs.title: Safety tethers
docs.text: Each crew member's tether starts at the airlock. As they translate, a routing point is added every ~16 m and removed when they pass back over it, so the yellow line follows the route they took. Seeking rebuilds the routing by replaying the path.

docs.title: Performance notes
docs.text:
• Truss lattices and solar-array masts are InstancedMesh batches (thousands of members, a handful of draw calls).
  • Textures are generated on canvases at start-up. The only downloads are three.js, fonts and three Earth maps.
  • HQ toggles shadow maps (4096² sun shadow), bloom and device-pixel-ratio rendering.

docs.title: Operations
docs.text:
The app's Operations browser lists every scenario newest first, grouped by month. You can filter it by type (Spacewalks, Vehicles, Robotics, Station), and each card is tagged Completed, Planned, Representative or Live, with a link to the NASA source where there is one.

Each mission is a script in src/data/missions.js. Times are Phase Elapsed Time (PET), counted from hatch opening, as in real EVA timelines. The tables below are generated from that file.

About the timing

US spacewalks typically last 6–7 hours. The PLSS is certified for about 8.5 hours and EMU crews pre-breathe pure oxygen first, because the suit runs at 4.3 psi. The station circles Earth every ~93 minutes, so a single EVA crosses three or four orbital nights. The sim starts each mission in the orbital morning, and the iROSA mission is timed so the roll-out happens in sunlight.

docs.title: iROSA Installation
docs.text:
US EVA · P6 truss · Power channel 2B · sim date 2021-06-20 · duration 6:30 (h:mm)

Modelled on the June 2021 spacewalks in which NASA’s Shane Kimbrough and ESA’s Thomas Pesquet installed the first ISS Roll-Out Solar Array over wing 2B.

Crew Suit Role EV1 EMU (red stripes) Red stripes · translates to the P6 worksite EV2 EMU Plain suit · rides Canadarm2 with the iROSA PET Phase What happens 0:00 Hatch open · egress Crew Lock depressurised to vacuum. EV1 opens the outward-opening hatch and leaves first, hooking the 85-ft safety tether reel. 0:12 Translate to P6 EV1 moves hand-over-hand over Quest and Destiny, onto the S0 truss and out along the port truss (≈ 50 m). 0:20 EV2 boards Canadarm2 EV2 ingresses the Articulating Portable Foot Restraint on the arm’s end effector. The arm already holds the iROSA, extracted from the Dragon trunk by ground controllers. 0:38 MBS translation to P3 The Mobile Transporter carries the MBS and Canadarm2 down the rails (≈ 2.5 cm/s) to the P3 worksite. 1:06 Arm fly-out Robotics officers fly EV2 and the 340 kg iROSA past the P4 arrays to the hand-off point. 1:40 iROSA hand-off EV2 releases the arm foot restraint and takes the iROSA; with EV1’s help it is hand-carried to the 2B mast canister. 2:08 Position on mod-kit bracket The iROSA is aligned to the modification-kit bracket installed on the mast canister during an earlier EVA. 2:30 Bolt & connect Bolts torqued with the Pistol Grip Tool; power and data cables mated to the existing channel 2B wiring. 3:16 Crew clear · unfold Crew moves clear of the deploy envelope. Release pins pulled, the two halves unfold. 3:20 Roll-out deploy Strain energy in the composite slit-tube booms unrolls the 19 m blanket in about 10 minutes — no motor needed. 3:32 Inspection & clean-up Photo documentation of the deployed iROSA, cable restraints, tool clean-up and tether checks. 4:22 Return to Quest EV2 leads the translation back. Canadarm2 and the MBS return to the S0 worksite. 5:50 Ingress EV2 then EV1 enter the Crew Lock. Hatch closed at PET ≈ 6:15; repressurisation ends the EVA.

docs.title: Li-ion Battery Swap
docs.text:
US EVA · S4 Integrated Equipment Assembly · sim date 2019-03-22 · duration 6:10 (h:mm)

Modelled on the 2017–2021 power-system upgrade spacewalks that replaced 48 nickel-hydrogen batteries with 24 lithium-ion ORUs and adapter plates on the four IEAs.

Crew Suit Role EV1 EMU (red stripes) Removes the old Ni-H₂ battery EV2 EMU Installs the new Li-ion ORU PET Phase What happens 0:00 Hatch open · egress Both crew members leave the Crew Lock and configure safety tethers, tools and the BRT (body restraint tether). 0:10 Translate to S4 Route over Quest and Destiny, up the S0 truss and out the starboard side past AMS-02 and ELC-2 (≈ 30 m). 0:20 MBS to S3 worksite Canadarm2, holding a new Li-ion battery pre-staged by Dextre, rides the Mobile Transporter to S3. 1:10 Arm to hand-off point The arm flies the 197 kg Li-ion ORU to just above the S4 IEA. 1:36 Remove Ni-H₂ battery EV1 drives the battery’s bolt with the Pistol Grip Tool and lifts it from slot B1. 1:40 Take new battery EV2 grasps the Li-ion ORU from the arm’s end effector. 1:54 Install Li-ion ORU EV2 slides the new battery into slot B1 and torques the bolt. 2:04 Old battery to arm EV1 hands the Ni-H₂ battery to Canadarm2 for transfer to the disposal pallet. 2:16 Adapter plate & connectors Adapter plate installed in the vacated slot; power and data connectors mated. 3:00 Power-up check Mission Control confirms the new battery is charging on channel 1A. 3:35 Get-ahead tasks Photo survey of the IEA and MLI clean-up while the timeline allows. 4:25 Return to Quest Translation back; the MBS and arm return to S0 with the old battery. 5:37 Ingress EV2 then EV1 ingress. Hatch closed, repressurisation.

Open this mission

docs.title: Nauka & ERA Outfitting
docs.text:
Russian EVA · Poisk airlock · Orlan-MKS suits · sim date 2022-04-18 · duration 6:15 (h:mm)

Modelled on the 2022 Roscosmos spacewalks that removed launch restraints from the European Robotic Arm, installed its control panel and checked it out on Nauka.

Crew Suit Role EV1 Orlan-MKS (red stripes) Orlan red stripes · EVA leader EV2 Orlan-MKS (blue stripes) Orlan blue stripes PET Phase What happens 0:00 Poisk hatch open After depressurising Poisk, the EVA leader opens the outward side hatch. Orlan suits run at 40 kPa (5.8 psi) — no long pre-breathe. 0:12 Translate to Nauka Hand-over-hand down Zvezda’s transfer compartment and onto Nauka, carrying the ERA control panel (IUPO). 0:56 Remove launch restraints Thermal covers and launch locks taken off the ERA joints and end effectors. 1:50 Install IUPO control panel The portable control panel lets an EVA cosmonaut command ERA from outside. 2:30 ERA checkout ERA is commanded through joint tests and a reach to a new pose while the crew monitors from a safe position. 3:35 Handrails & cables Handrails installed and cable runs routed to Nauka’s external experiment ports. 4:25 Photo survey Inspection photos of Nauka’s hull and clean-up of tools. 5:00 Return to Poisk Translation back up Zvezda to the Poisk hatch. 5:44 Ingress Both cosmonauts back in Poisk; hatch closed and repressurised.

docs.title: SpaceX CRS-35 Docking (visiting vehicle)
docs.text:
Cargo Dragon · Harmony zenith (IDA-3) · Oct 2026 · sim date 2026-10-15 · duration 2:40 (h:mm)

NASA’s 35th SpaceX resupply mission launched on a Falcon 9 from SLC-40 on 13 Oct 2026 and docked autonomously to Harmony’s space-facing port on 15 Oct after about 51 hours of phasing. It carries more than 6,300 lb of science and supplies, including the final pair of iROSAs, and stays about a month.

Launch Falcon 9 · SLC-40 · 13 Oct 2026 Port Harmony zenith (IDA-3) Cargo > 6,300 lb science & supplies Trunk Final iROSA pair Stay ≈ 1 month · Pacific splashdown PET Phase What happens 0:00 Approach ellipsoid After ≈ 51 hours of phasing, Dragon enters the 4 × 2 × 2 km approach ellipsoid behind and below the station, talking to it over the proximity link. 0:25 Waypoint 0 Dragon holds about 400 m below the station. NASA and SpaceX poll “go” for entering the 200 m Keep-Out Sphere. 0:40 Keep-Out Sphere entry Dragon swings around the station’s forward side toward the zenith docking axis, firing its Draco thrusters in short pulses. 1:00 Waypoint 1 Holding ≈ 220 m directly above Harmony on the docking axis. Dragon aligns its nose with IDA-3 using its LIDAR and cameras. 1:10 Approach to Waypoint 2 Dragon closes down the approach corridor at ≈ 0.15 m/s. 1:30 Waypoint 2 Final hold 20 m from the port. Last go / no-go; the crew stand by to command a hold, retreat or abort. 1:40 Final approach Dragon closes the last 20 m autonomously at a few centimetres per second. 1:46 Soft capture Contact with the International Docking Adapter on Harmony’s space-facing port; capture latches engage. 1:56 Hard capture Twelve structural hooks close to form a rigid, sealed connection. 2:00 Leak checks The vestibule between Dragon and IDA-3 is pressurised and checked for leaks. 2:32 Hatch open The crew open the hatch and start unloading: LambdaVision-1, Stellar Spheroids, ELF-Unconventional Glass 2, MINDS and station hardware. Canadarm2 will later extract the iROSA pair from the trunk.

Open this mission

Dragon follows the standard rendezvous profile: Waypoint 0 below the station, a fly-around outside the 200 m Keep-Out Sphere, Waypoint 1 (≈ 220 m) and Waypoint 2 (20 m) on the docking axis, then autonomous final approach. The Zones toggle shows the Keep-Out Sphere and approach corridor; Centerline cam looks up the docking axis from IDA-3.

Sources: NASA CRS-35 mission overview, Space.com docking coverage.

docs.title: Canadarm2 & Dextre: antenna swap (robotics)
docs.text:
Robotics · Ku-band antenna ORU on Z1 · no spacewalk · sim date 2026-10-21 · duration 4:00 (h:mm)

A representative Mobile Servicing System task, not a replay of one dated event. Ground controllers in Houston and at CSA in Saint-Hubert command Canadarm2 to pick up Dextre, fetch a spare from an ExPRESS Logistics Carrier and swap a failed Ku-band antenna boom on the Z1 truss. This is how many ORUs (batteries, cameras, pumps) are now replaced without a spacewalk.

Arm Canadarm2 (SSRMS) · 17.6 m · 7 joints Hand Dextre (SPDM) · two 3.35 m arms Base MBS on the Mobile Transporter Task Ku-band antenna ORU swap on Z1 Spare From ExPRESS Logistics Carrier 2 (S3) Control Ground-commanded · NASA & CSA PET Phase What happens 0:00 Robotics ops begin Ground controllers take the arm out of its park position. The crew is not needed; the whole job is commanded from Earth over the Ku/S-band links. 0:12 Approach Dextre Canadarm2 flies its Latching End Effector over Dextre’s grapple fixture on the Mobile Base System. 0:25 Grapple Dextre Snare wires close on the grapple pin and the LEE rigidises. Dextre is released from the MBS and now hangs from the end of the arm. 0:40 MBS to S3 The Mobile Transporter carries the MBS, Canadarm2 and Dextre down the rails to the S3 worksite (≈ 2.5 cm/s). 1:05 Fetch the spare The arm positions Dextre over ExPRESS Logistics Carrier 2 on the S3 truss. 1:15 Extract new antenna ORU Dextre’s right arm drives its OTCM gripper onto the spare’s fixture and unbolts it from the carrier. 1:35 Back to S0 MBS returns to the S0 worksite; the arm carries Dextre and the spare toward the Z1 truss on top of Unity. 2:20 Remove failed antenna Dextre’s left arm grips the failed Ku-band boom-and-dish ORU, releases its bolt and pulls it off the Z1 interface plate. 2:38 Reposition Canadarm2 shifts Dextre about 3 m so the right arm, holding the spare, lines up with the empty interface. 2:48 Install new antenna The new ORU is inserted and its bolt driven. Power and data connect through the interface. 3:10 Link checkout Flight controllers power the antenna, slew its gimbal and check the Ku-band link through a Tracking and Data Relay Satellite. 3:25 Stow & return The failed unit is stowed on Dextre’s ORU platform for return on a later cargo flight. Dextre goes back to the MBS and the arm returns to park.

Open this mission

The arm, Dextre's two arms and the hand-offs use the same keyframe and attachment system as the spacewalks: Dextre rides the arm's end effector, Dextre's hands follow invisible markers, and each antenna unit rides a hand. Views: Canadarm2 follows the end effector, Dextre follows the robot, LEE cam looks down past the end effector.

docs.title: Final iROSA Installs
docs.text:
US EVA · Menon & Kutryk · Oct 29 & Nov 5, 2026 · sim date 2026-10-29 · duration 6:30 (h:mm)

NASA’s Anil Menon and CSA’s Joshua Kutryk are scheduled to install the last roll-out solar arrays, delivered by CRS-35, in spacewalks on 29 Oct and 5 Nov 2026, finishing the power upgrade (“up to 30 percent” more generation). NASA has not said which wing comes first; the sim shows wing 2A on P4, and which crew member rides the arm is illustrative.

Crew Suit Role EV1 EMU (red stripes) Translates to the P4 worksite EV2 EMU Rides Canadarm2 with the iROSA PET Phase What happens 0:00 Hatch open · egress Crew Lock depressurised; both spacewalkers leave Quest and set up safety tethers. Menon configured the tools and inspected the tethers in Quest beforehand. 0:12 Translate to P4 EV1 moves hand-over-hand along the port truss to the P4 power module (≈ 35 m). 0:20 EV2 boards Canadarm2 EV2 ingresses the foot restraint on the arm, which holds one of the two iROSAs CRS-35 delivered in Dragon’s trunk. 0:38 MBS to P3 The Mobile Transporter carries the arm to the P3 worksite. 1:06 Arm fly-over Robotics officers fly EV2 and the iROSA over the truss to the aft side of P4, where wing 2A extends. 1:40 Hand-off EV2 leaves the arm and carries the iROSA to the 2A mast canister with EV1. 2:08 Mount on bracket The iROSA is aligned with the modification-kit bracket on the mast canister. 2:30 Bolt & connect Bolts torqued and cables mated to channel 2A. 3:16 Crew clear · unfold Crew moves clear of the deploy envelope and the two halves unfold. 3:20 Roll-out deploy The blanket unrolls in about 10 minutes, driven by the stored strain energy in its booms. 3:32 Inspection & clean-up Photo survey, cable restraints and tool clean-up. The second spacewalk on 5 Nov installs the other iROSA. 4:22 Return to Quest Translation back; Canadarm2 and the MBS return to S0. 5:50 Ingress Both crew back in the Crew Lock; hatch closed, repressurisation.

docs.title: Z1 Antenna Replacement
docs.text:
US EVA · Menon & Adenot · Aug 25, 2026 · 6 h 30 min · sim date 2026-08-25 · duration 6:30 (h:mm)

NASA’s Anil Menon and ESA’s Sophie Adenot spent 6 hours 30 minutes replacing a failed high-speed space-to-ground antenna with a spare on the Z1 truss above Unity, then made the connections to activate it. Menon worked from a foot restraint on Canadarm2’s end effector. Where the spare and the failed unit were stowed is illustrative.

Crew Suit Role Adenot EMU ESA · works from the Z1 truss Menon EMU (red stripes) NASA · rides Canadarm2 (stripes illustrative) PET Phase What happens 0:00 Hatch open · egress Both spacewalkers leave the Quest Crew Lock and set up their safety tethers. 0:12 Adenot to Z1 Adenot climbs over Quest and Unity to the top of the Z1 truss, where the antenna boom stands. 0:20 Menon on Canadarm2 Menon ingresses the foot restraint on Canadarm2’s latching end effector. The spare antenna rides alongside on the arm. 0:40 Arm to the worksite Robotics officers fly Menon and the spare over the S0 truss to the Z1 antenna. 1:02 Disconnect failed antenna Connectors demated and the boom’s attachment bolt released. 1:35 Remove failed antenna Menon lifts the failed boom-and-dish unit off the Z1 interface plate while on the arm. 1:50 Install the spare The arm positions the spare on the interface plate; Adenot guides it in and drives the bolt. 2:04 Connect & activate Power and data connectors mated so flight controllers can activate the new antenna. 2:55 Stow failed unit The arm carries Menon and the failed antenna back over S0, where it is temporarily stowed. 3:50 Get-ahead tasks Clean-up and photo documentation while the timeline allows. 4:50 Return to Quest Both crew translate back to the airlock. 5:58 Ingress Hatch closed at about 6 h 20 min; repressurisation ends the 6 h 30 min spacewalk.

docs.title: Cygnus XL Release
docs.text:
Canadarm2 unberths Cygnus · Unity Earth-facing port · Oct 9, 2026 · sim date 2026-10-09 · duration 2:10 (h:mm)

After nearly six months berthed to Unity’s Earth-facing port, Northrop Grumman’s Cygnus XL was detached and released by Canadarm2 at 12:44 p.m. EDT on 9 Oct 2026, about 260 miles above the Pacific. It had delivered about 11,000 lb of cargo and left with several thousand pounds of disposal items for a destructive re-entry after its 12 Oct deorbit. The arm’s base point and the release distance are illustrative.

Operator Northrop Grumman Port Unity Earth-facing (nadir) Delivered ≈ 11,000 lb of cargo Berthed Nearly six months Release 12:44 p.m. EDT · 9 Oct 2026 Deorbit 12 Oct · burns up with trash PET Phase What happens 0:00 Grapple Cygnus Canadarm2, working from a base point on the US Lab, latches onto Cygnus’s grapple fixture. 0:12 Unbolt from Unity The Common Berthing Mechanism bolts that held Cygnus to Unity’s Earth-facing port are driven out. 0:40 Unberth The arm pulls Cygnus straight out of the berthing port. 0:48 Maneuver to release Robotics controllers fly Cygnus away from the station to the release position below Unity. 1:10 Release position Cygnus holds on the end of the arm while teams confirm “go” for release. 1:22 Release · 12:44 p.m. EDT The end effector opens and Cygnus floats free, about 260 miles above the Pacific Ocean. 1:28 Arm backs away Canadarm2 retreats while Cygnus drifts away from the station. 1:35 Departure burns Cygnus fires its thrusters to leave the station’s vicinity. Deorbit follows on 12 Oct; it burns up over the ocean with its disposal cargo.

Open this mission

These three operations come from NASA's Space Station blog (Expedition 75). Where NASA did not publish a detail (which wing gets the first 2026 iROSA, where the failed antenna was stowed, Canadarm2's base point for the Cygnus release), the sim makes an illustrative choice and says so in the app.

docs.text:
No crew outside. The station is shown in its current configuration (six iROSAs, Nauka, Prichal, Bishop) and loops one orbit. The SARJs turn once per revolution, the Beta Gimbals trim each wing for the beta angle, and the radiators turn edge-on to the Sun.

docs.title: Writing a new mission
docs.text:
A mission is a plain object:

{
  id: 'my-eva', title: '…', subtitle: '…', inspiration: '…',
  epoch: '2024-01-01T12:00:00Z',   // sets Sun position & Earth rotation
  raan: 120,                        // orbit plane orientation (deg)
  duration: 390,                    // minutes
  airlock: 'quest',                 // 'quest' | 'poisk' — tether anchor & hatch
  config: { nauka: true, pirs: false, prichal: true, bishop: true,
            irosa: ['2B', '4B'], vehicles: ['dragon', 'soyuz', 'progress'] },
  crew: [{ id: 'ev1', role: 'EV1', suit: 'emu', stripes: 'red', note: '…' }],
  phases: [{ t: 0, title: 'Hatch open', detail: '…' }],
  tracks: {
    ev1: [ /* { t, p:[x,y,z], face?, up?, belly? } */ ],
    arm: [ /* Canadarm2 end-effector keys */ ],
    era: [ /* ERA end-effector keys */ ],
  },
  scalars: { mbs: [[t, z]], hatch: [[t, 0..1]] },
  payloads: [{ id, kind: 'battery' | 'batteryOld' | 'irosaPackage' | 'panel', keys, show }],
  attach:   [{ who, to, from, until, off:[x,y,z], face?, up?, mode? }],
}
  • Positions are station-frame metres (x forward, y zenith, z starboard). The helpers route() and trussTopRoute() lay out hand-over-hand paths along the truss, including climbing over AMS-02, the ELCs and the IEAs.
  • attach lets one thing ride another: an astronaut on the arm's foot restraint, a battery in a crew member's hands. Boundary keys are inserted automatically, so hand-offs glide rather than jump.
  • While a crew member is moving they translate head-first, with belly (default nadir) facing the structure. When stationary they use face and up.

docs.title: Station reference
docs.text: The model is built from published dimensions. Every element below can be clicked in the app to open the same data in the inspector panel (src/data/components.js).

docs.title: Whole station
docs.text: Span 109 m (truss) × 73 m (module stack incl. visiting vehicles) Mass ≈ 420,000 kg Pressurised volume 916 m³ (388 m³ habitable) Orbit ≈ 415 km, 51.64° inclination, 92.7 min period, 7.66 km/s Continuously crewed Since 2 November 2000

docs.title: Coordinate frame
docs.text:
The scene uses the ISS local-vertical / local-horizontal frame, mapped onto three.js axes:

three.js ISS body / LVLH Direction +x +X Forward, along the velocity vector (Harmony, PMA-2) +y −Z Zenith, away from Earth +z +Y Starboard, along the starboard truss

docs.title: Logistics Twin
docs.text:
A 3D digital twin of an e-commerce fulfilment centre. A simulation runs a full day of operations, from the supplier truck at the inbound door to the line-haul trailer leaving for another city. You can watch every robot, reach truck, parcel and trailer, change how the site is run, and see the effect on throughput, cost and service.

Open Logistics Twin Source on GitHub

docs.title: The site
docs.text:
An illustrative 132 × 84 m building near Mumbai, with eight destination lanes: Mumbai, Pune, Nashik, Surat, Ahmedabad, Goa, Indore and Hyderabad.

Zone What it holds Inbound yard and doors 8 dock doors with levellers and dock lights, yard stalls for trucks waiting for a door Receiving Staging lanes behind each door where pallets are unloaded Reserve racking 7 double rows, 13 bays, 5 levels: 910 pallet positions served by reach trucks AMR pick zone 2 blocks × 6 rows of shelving with 480 pick faces, one SKU each; carton stock is visible and drains as it is picked Charging 10 robot chargers Pack stations Up to 12 stations, each with a packer, monitor and packing table Sorter Conveyor along the north wall with diverts into 8 destination lanes Outbound docks 8 doors, one per destination, with line-haul trailers

docs.title: How the operation works
docs.text:
Supplier truck → door → unload (95 s/pallet) → staging → reach truck putaway → reserve rack
                                                                   │
                                     replenishment when a face drops below 18 units
                                                                   ▼
Customer order → queue → AMR (1 order or a batch) → pick faces (zone picker loads tote)
       → pack station → sorter → destination lane → trailer (wave loading) → departure
  • Demand: orders arrive as a Poisson process whose rate follows an hour-of-day profile.
    • Each order has 1–4 lines, and 480 SKUs follow a Pareto curve: about 20% of SKUs make up 80% of lines.
    • Each order gets a destination by city share and a ship-within promise (4 h by default).
  • Robots (AMRs):
    • Routing: they plan routes with A* on a 1 m grid of the floor, smoothed by line of sight, and keep to the right in aisles.
    • Picking: they sequence pick stops with a nearest-neighbour rule that knows about aisles. They can take one order per trip or a batch of 2–6 orders.
    • Battery: drains while driving and picking. Robots charge when low, and opportunistically when idle.
  • Slotting:
    • ABC slotting places the fastest movers nearest packing. Random slotting shows the cost of not doing so: robot travel per order rises from about 75 m to about 120 m.
    • Putaway is also class-aware: A items go low and close, C items high and far.
  • Packing: each station takes 34 s plus 7 s per line, and robots choose the station with the shortest queue.
  • Outbound: each destination has a trailer every two hours. Loading starts 35 minutes before departure, so parcels visibly build up in the lanes. A full trailer leaves early and an extra trailer is called.

docs.title: KPIs and bottlenecks
docs.text:
The dashboard updates live:

  • Throughput: shipped orders per hour; open orders by stage (to pick, picking, packing, sorter, at the dock).
  • Service:
    • order-to-packed cycle time
    • on-time % (orders that are open and already past their promise count as late)
    • fill rate
  • Efficiency:
    • robot travel per order
    • dock-to-stock time
    • utilisation of AMRs, pack stations, reach trucks and inbound doors
    • racking fill
  • Cost per order: an illustrative ₹ running cost (robots, pickers, packers, reach trucks, dock crews and fixed site cost) divided by orders shipped.
  • Charts: orders in vs shipped per 15 minutes, and open orders against utilisation.

A rule-based bottleneck finder flags saturated packing, saturated robots, a forklift backlog, trucks queuing in the yard, empty pick faces, racking running out of space, SLA risk and low batteries. Most findings have an Apply button that makes the fix live, for example +2 pack stations or switch to batch picking.

docs.title: Scenarios
docs.text: Scenario What to look for Normal weekday ~220 orders/hour, balanced flow with packing running at about 75–85% Festive sale peak 2.6× demand with the normal crew: packing and robots saturate, open orders climb into the thousands, the on-time rate drops Festive peak, scaled up 30 AMRs on batch picking, 12 pack stations and 7 reach trucks keep cycle time to a few minutes Dock disruption One inbound door for 26-pallet trucks: trucks queue in the yard and the racking fills Random slotting Same demand, robots travel ~60% further per order and utilisation rises

docs.title: Van Maharashtra · Forests and industrial projects
docs.text:
Maharashtra's forest cover in 3D from 2021 to 2050. An illustrative pipeline of mines, plants, roads, railways, dams, industrial estates and ports takes forest land, thins the forest around it and breaks the corridors between tiger reserves. Three scenarios show how much depends on how projects are sited and mitigated.

Open Van Maharashtra Source on GitHub

Illustrative, not a forecast

The 2021 totals follow the Forest Survey of India's India State of Forest Report (ISFR) 2021. Where the forest lies is a smoothed sketch, not the FSI map.

The projects are illustrative types placed in real forest regions, not actual proposals or approvals. The clearing, thinning, planting and survival rates are assumptions chosen to compare scenarios.

For real figures see the FSI's reports and the PARIVESH portal.

docs.title: The 2021 baseline
docs.text:
Class (canopy density) Area Share of the state Very dense forest (over 70%) 8,734 km² 2.8% Moderately dense forest (40–70%) 20,589 km² 6.7% Open forest (10–40%) 21,475 km² 7.0% Forest cover 50,798 km² 16.5% of 307,713 km²

The state is cut into 8,867 cells of about 6 × 6 km, each holding a share of the three classes. The main tracts are:

  • East and north: Gadchiroli, Chandrapur–Tadoba, Gondia–Bhandara (Navegaon–Nagzira), Pench and Umred, Melghat, Yavatmal–Kinwat, and the Satpura in Nandurbar and Jalgaon.
  • West: Nashik–Thane–Palghar, the Sahyadri from Igatpuri to Tillari, and the Konkan mangroves.

The Nagpur division holds about half the state's forest.

docs.title: What happens each year
docs.text:
1. Clearing: each project takes its forest land from the cells it sits on, or along its route for roads and railways.
  2. Thinning: for ten years, the forest around a project loses density from edge effects, new access, fuelwood and grazing. Very dense forest becomes moderately dense, and moderately dense becomes open. Some open forest is cleared outright for new roads and settlement.
  3. Background: dense forest thins slowly statewide. In the Avoid scenario, restoration also adds open cover.
  4. Compensatory afforestation: an equal area is planted after a lag.
  5. Saplings are not forest cover.
  6. A plantation counts as open forest after 5 years (if it survives) and as moderately dense after 20.
  7. Under business as usual it is planted on degraded land far away, in Marathwada, which is why that division gains cover while the others lose it.
  8. Corridors: each is scored against 2021 from the forest along it. Roads and railways cut it (less so with wildlife crossings), and so do mines and plants nearby.

docs.title: Three scenarios
docs.text:
By 2050 Business as usual Avoid and mitigate High growth Forest cover 49,320 km² (−1,478) 52,646 km² (+1,848) 45,773 km² (−5,025) Share of the state 16.0% 17.1% 14.9% Very dense forest −20.6% −3.3% −38.1% Cleared directly for projects 286 km² 81 km² 612 km² Thinned around projects 3,418 km² 196 km² 7,883 km² Open forest lost to access and settlement 1,350 km² 77 km² 4,008 km² Forest carbon −24 Mt C +7 Mt C −61 Mt C Projects built 24 18 (6 dropped) 48 Tadoba–Gadchiroli–Indravati corridor 69 / 100 88 / 100 56 / 100

The land cleared directly is small: about 0.6% of the state's forest under business as usual. The damage is mostly elsewhere:

  • dense forest thinning around each project;
  • the open forest lost to the roads and settlements that follow;
  • corridors broken where projects cluster, as in the Wardha valley and the Gadchiroli hills.

Plantations add area but not old forest. Total cover can look steady while the densest forest disappears.

The Change layer turns each tile red where forest was lost and orange where dense forest thinned.

docs.title: The project pipeline
docs.text:
24 illustrative projects from 2022 to 2036 cover iron-ore, limestone and bauxite mines, open-cast coal, plants and an ash pond, highways and railways, dams, industrial estates and a port.

Each has a year, the forest land it seeks, and what the Avoid scenario does with it:

  • drop it if it is in a tiger reserve, corridor or the Western Ghats;
  • shift it to non-forest land;
  • shrink it by 40%;
  • or add wildlife crossings to a road or railway.

The Projects tab lists them with the forest each actually took. Clicking one flies to it, or to its close-up site.

docs.title: Close-up sites
docs.text: Site What you see Iron-ore mine, Gadchiroli The pit is dug into the hill bench by bench. Waste dumps grow, haul trucks run, a haul road cuts the forest and the forest around thins. A compensatory plantation grows in rows beside the lease, with gaps where saplings died. Under Avoid the proposal is dropped and the forest stays. Highway through the Pench corridor A strip of forest goes for a four-lane road with traffic. With no crossings, deer turn back at the edge; under Avoid, three underpasses keep the forest continuous and animals cross beneath. Dam in a Melghat valley The wall rises, then the reservoir fills over four years and drowns the valley forest. Under Avoid it is dropped. Port on the Palghar mangroves The creek is reclaimed in stages, removing mangroves and mudflat; container yards and cranes follow.

docs.title: The law, in brief
docs.text:
• Diversion approval: using forest land for non-forest purposes needs central approval under the Forest (Conservation) Act, 1980. It was renamed the Van (Sanrakshan Evam Samvardhan) Adhiniyam in 2023.
  • Payments: user agencies pay for compensatory afforestation and the net present value of the forest lost, into funds managed under the Compensatory Afforestation Fund Act, 2016 (CAMPA).
  • Community rights: the Forest Rights Act, 2006 recognises the rights of forest-dwelling communities.
  • Wildlife clearances: tiger reserves, sanctuaries and eco-sensitive zones need these in addition.

docs.title: Urja Maharashtra · State power grid
docs.text:
Maharashtra's electricity system in 3D, from plant to plug. Power is dispatched every 15 minutes and followed through the three state companies:

  • Mahagenco (MSPGCL) generates;
  • Mahapareshan (MSETCL) carries it at 765, 400 and 220 kV;
  • Mahavitaran (MSEDCL) delivers it to homes, industry and farm pumps.

Open Urja Maharashtra Source on GitHub

Note

The model is simplified and illustrative. Capacities, locations, costs, demand and the network are approximate. State Load Despatch Centre (SLDC) reports, Maharashtra Electricity Regulatory Commission (MERC) orders and the companies' own reports govern.

docs.title: From plant to plug
docs.text:
Company Role In the app Mahagenco, Maharashtra State Power Generation Co. Owns the state's own power stations Coal at Chandrapur, Koradi, Khaperkheda, Bhusawal, Parli, Nashik and Paras; Uran gas; Koyna hydro; Ghatghar pumped storage; Sakri solar Mahapareshan, Maharashtra State Electricity Transmission Co. Runs the EHV network and the SLDC at Airoli 20 substations, 765/400/220 kV lines, the Chandrapur–Padghe HVDC link and the ties to five neighbouring states Mahavitaran, Maharashtra State Electricity Distribution Co. Supplies every consumer outside Mumbai island 13 load areas plus the Mumbai licensees (BEST, Tata Power, Adani Electricity), each split into industry, homes, commercial and farm pumps

The three companies were formed in 2005, when the Maharashtra State Electricity Board was split under MSEB Holding Co.

Other stations supply the rest:

  • Private: Tiroda, Ratnagiri, Amravati, Dahanu, Trombay and the Tata hydros.
  • Central, in the state: Mauda, Solapur and Tarapur.
  • Renewable developers: wind on the Satara and Dhule ridges, solar parks, MSKVY 2.0 farm-feeder solar and rooftop solar.
  • From outside the state: its share of central stations elsewhere, and the power exchange.

docs.title: The map
docs.text:
The relief shows the Konkan coast, the Sahyadri (Western Ghats), the Deccan plateau and the Satpura, with the Godavari, Krishna, Koyna, Tapi and Wainganga rivers.

  • Stations: each has a small model, a column showing its output now inside a faint sleeve for its capacity, and a ring for its owner (orange Mahagenco, grey private, blue central, green renewable).
  • Lines: coloured by voltage, on towers. Dots run along each line in the direction of flow: green below 60% of rating, amber to 90%, red above. Arrows at the border show the flow on each tie.
  • Cities: clusters of buildings that light up at night, labelled with their demand.

Views: Maharashtra, Vidarbha, Mumbai–Konkan, Pune–Koyna and Marathwada. Clicking a station in the Mahagenco tab flies to it.

docs.title: Six close-up sites
docs.text: Site What you see Koradi coal station Three 660 MW units, each with a boiler house, chimney and cooling tower. Smoke and steam follow each unit's output. Also a coal yard with a stacker-reclaimer, the conveyor to the bunkers, a coal train, generator transformers and the switchyard. Koyna dam Shivajisagar lake (its level follows the season), the gravity dam with radial spillway gates that open in the monsoon, the intake, penstocks and a powerhouse whose tailrace churns with output. MSKVY solar plant Single-axis trackers following the sun beside a 33/11 kV substation, and farm feeders to pump houses that spray water while the feeder is on. Satara wind ridge Eight turbines turning with the season's wind; the monsoon runs them hardest. Padghe The 400 kV yard with transformers and bays that feeds Mumbai and Thane, and the HVDC valve hall, converter transformers and DC line from Chandrapur. Mahavitaran distribution A 33/11 kV substation, a town feeder with pole-mounted transformers, houses (some with rooftop solar), an EV charger and street lights, and a farm feeder to pumps.

docs.title: How it is simulated
docs.text:
Demand: each area's demand is built from four profiles (industry, homes, commercial and farm pumps) and scaled to a season's peak.

Season Peak Energy in a day Summer 29.5 GW about 534 GWh Monsoon 23.5 GW about 450 GWh Winter 27 GW about 496 GWh

Farm pumps run in day and night rotations, or mostly by day with MSKVY 2.0.

Dispatch: every 15-minute block, as SLDC schedules.

  1. Solar, wind and nuclear run first.
  2. Koyna's daily water budget goes on the highest net-load hours (7 GWh a day in summer, 30 GWh in the monsoon). Ghatghar pumps in the solar trough and generates at the evening peak.
  3. Coal and gas, the central share and the power exchange fill the rest in merit order (lowest variable cost first).
  4. Coal units can't go below a 55% minimum technical load.
  5. Coal ramps at most 12% of capacity a block.
  6. The central share stays at or above 55%.
  7. Exchange purchases change by at most 600 MW a block.
  8. The exchange price follows a day shape: cheap in the solar hours, dear in the evening.
  9. Any surplus curtails solar and wind. Any shortfall is drawn from the national grid as a deviation.

Flows: a DC load flow on the network gives every line's flow. The Mahapareshan tab also runs an N-1 check: it trips one circuit of each line in turn and reports the worst loading that results.

Frequency: losing generation dips the national grid's frequency. Primary response arrests the fall within seconds, and automatic generation control (AGC) restores it over a few minutes.

Losing a 660 MW unit at full load gives a nadir of about 49.91 Hz. Maharashtra's overdrawal until the next block is charged under the Deviation Settlement Mechanism (DSM).

docs.title: Scenarios
docs.text: Scenario What happens Heatwave Afternoon and evening demand rises 8% with air-conditioning; the exchange and the peaking plants work harder. Solar agri feeders (MSKVY 2.0) On by default. 4,000 MW of solar near substations feeds farm feeders by day, and the pumping load moves from night rotations into daylight. Trip a 660 MW unit at Koradi The unit's output (≈360 MW at a noon backing-down level) is lost at once. Frequency dips, Maharashtra overdraws until the next block, then SLDC re-dispatches. HVDC Chandrapur–Padghe outage The 1,200 MW the link was carrying west reroutes over the AC network. The busiest line in a summer day goes from 79% to 90% of its rating. Trip Aurangabad–Pune 765 kV The main east–west 765 kV line trips and flows shift to the 400 kV corridors. Coal shortage at Chandrapur The state's largest station is held to 60%; more is bought from the exchange. Cloud bank over Marathwada Eastern solar drops 70% for the afternoon; coal and the exchange cover it.

docs.title: Solar agri feeders: night rotation against MSKVY 2.0
docs.text:
The System tab runs the season's day both ways, with the same farm energy. For a summer day:

Night rotation MSKVY 2.0 Power purchase cost ₹170.5 crore ₹170.3 crore CO₂ 391,139 t 371,268 t Coal generation 299,641 MWh 279,875 MWh Peak demand (at noon) 26.4 GW 29.5 GW Solar curtailed 209 MWh 1,742 MWh

Moving pumping into daylight lets 4,000 MW of local solar serve it. Coal burn falls by about 20 GWh and CO₂ by about 20,000 t a day.

The noon peak is higher, but the sun covers it. Some solar is curtailed at midday, which storage or more flexible coal would recover.

docs.title: कुंभनगरी · Kumbh City
docs.text:
A 3D crowd and transport simulator of Nashik during the Simhastha Kumbh Mela. You plan the city for a normal mela day, a parva snan or an Amrit Snan, then watch lakhs of pilgrims park, ride shuttles, walk to the Godavari, bathe and go home. A report at the end of the day shows what worked.

Open Kumbh City Source on GitHub

docs.title: The Simhastha
docs.text:
The Kumbh Mela comes to Nashik and Trimbakeshwar every 12 years, when Jupiter is in Leo (Simha). For the 2027 mela the Amrit Snan (royal bath) days at Nashik are 2 August, 31 August and 11 September 2027. Nashik's plan for the crowds has three tiers:

  1. Outer parking hubs on every highway. There are also special trains to Nashik Road (and Deolali).
  2. Electric shuttle buses from the hubs to transfer points at the edge of the city.
  3. A vehicle-free zone around the ghats, which pilgrims cross on foot.

Kumbh City models this plan. Its map is stylised, with the places in the right relation to each other:

  • Panchavati on the north bank, with Ramkund, Kalaram temple and Kapaleshwar.
  • Old Nashik across the Ahilyabai Holkar bridge.
  • Tapovan and its Sadhugram downstream, where the Kapila joins the Godavari.
  • Dasak and Nashik Road to the south-east.

docs.title: How the simulation works
docs.text:
Pilgrims move in groups of 250. Each group:

  1. arrives by road at a parking hub, or by train, following the day's arrival profile
  2. picks a ghat and a transfer point
  3. queues for a shuttle (or walks if the queue is longer than the walk)
  4. walks through the streets to the ghat
  5. queues and takes a holy dip
  6. may visit Kalaram for darshan
  7. walks back and takes the shuttle home

The model behind each step:

  • Walking speed falls as a street gets crowded, following Weidmann's speed–density relation. A street that is full makes people wait behind it, so queues back up towards the transfer points. Above 4 people/m² is counted as critical crowding.
  • People walking in opposite directions on one street slow each other down.
  • Ghats bathe 60 people per metre of frontage per hour.
  • Parking fills up as vehicles stay for the whole visit. When it's full, arrivals back up on the highways.
  • On Amrit Snan days the three Vaishnav akharas process from Tapovan before dawn and bathe at Ramkund from about 06:20. Ramkund, Laxmankund and Gadge Maharaj ghat are reserved for them from 04:00 to 09:30, and the procession route is closed to the public.

docs.text:
