You can change the crowd size from 1 to 80 lakh.

docs.title: Planning
docs.text:
Every measure has an illustrative cost against a ₹600 crore budget.

Measure What it does Ghat frontage Add 50 m at a time to any of nine ghats. Tapovan and Dasak have the most room; Ramkund very little. Someshwar ghat Open an upstream site with its own access road. Electric shuttles 300–4,500 buses, shared between hubs by demand. Peth Road and Gangapur Road hubs Each adds parking for 12,000 vehicles. Deolali special trains Split rail pilgrims between two stations. Vehicle-free core Keeps private cars out, so shuttles run at about 20 km/h instead of 11. One-way circulation Separate in and out routes around the ghats. Holding areas Large pandals at transfer points. People are let in only when the route ahead and the ghat queue have room, and shuttles pause when a holding area fills. ICCC & CCTV The command centre sends each group to the ghat with the shortest total time, diverts people away from Ramkund while it is reserved, and moves idle buses to the busiest hubs. Widen the Ramkund footbridge / Kalaram Road Fixes the two narrowest approaches. Tapovan pontoon bridge A floating bridge linking Dwarka to the Kapila sangam. Toilets, medical posts Sanitation and medical response time. Gangapur dam release Keeps the river flowing, so water quality at Ramkund stays higher.

Suggest a plan loads a strong plan for the Amrit Snan. Switch single measures off to see what each one contributes: holding areas, for example, remove most critical crowding.

docs.title: Harit Ghar · Polyhouse and vertical farm
docs.text:
A polyhouse and a vertical farm in 3D, run by IoT sensors and AI. A live climate model drives both. You can run them by hand, with the fixed rules of a typical controller, or with an AI that plans ahead, catches faults and spots disease early.

Open Harit Ghar Source on GitHub

Note

The equipment is generic. The climate physics and crop figures are simplified and illustrative, and the AI's vision detections are simulated. Crop advisories, makers' data and current scheme guidelines govern.

docs.title: Two facilities
docs.text:
Polyhouse Vertical farm Type Naturally ventilated polyhouse (NVPH) with fan-and-pad cooling Insulated indoor room with NFT racks under LEDs Size 3 bays × 8 m × 40 m = 960 m², gutter 4.5 m, ridge 6.6 m 14 × 20 m room; 4 racks × 6 tiers × 16 m = 461 m² growing area Crops Coloured capsicum, indeterminate tomato, parthenocarpic cucumber Butterhead lettuce, Genovese basil, baby spinach Climate kit Roll-up side curtains behind 40-mesh net, ridge vent flaps, 50% aluminised shade screen, 6 exhaust fans and a 23 m cellulose pad wall, 6 fogging lines LEDs at 2.8 µmol/J, 60 kW HVAC, dehumidifier, CO₂ dosing, rack fans Water Drip on 12 beds; fertigation with stock tanks A, B and acid NFT channels; dosing pumps, UV steriliser, chiller; condensate recovered Network LoRaWAN to a gateway on a pole Wi-Fi to an edge gateway, MQTT

The two facilities run on the same clock all the time. Switch between them from the left panel.

docs.title: The climate model
docs.text:
Both facilities step forward one simulated minute at a time. The models are deliberately simple, but each effect pushes the right way.

Polyhouse: an energy, water-vapour and CO₂ balance per m² of floor.

  • Sun: solar gain through the 200 µm cover (72% transmission), cut by up to half when the shade screen is closed.
  • Natural ventilation: through the side curtains and ridge vents, driven by wind and by the inside-outside temperature difference.
  • Fan-and-pad cooling: air leaves the wet pad 80% of the way from the outside temperature to the wet-bulb temperature, picking up moisture. Open vents short-circuit the pad.
  • Fogging: evaporates only while the air is dry enough. The rest wets the leaves.
  • Crop: transpiration rises with light and VPD. Photosynthesis responds to light, CO₂, temperature and VPD.
  • Beds: substrate moisture is tracked per bed, with drainage. Feed EC is tracked for the fertigation.

Vertical farm:

  • Heat and water: LED heat splits into sensible heat and transpiration.
  • HVAC: cooling with a COP that falls as it gets hotter outside. The coil and dehumidifier remove water, and the condensate goes back to the tank.
  • CO₂: dosed to the setpoint while lit; lost through leakage.
  • Nutrients: EC drifts up as plants drink, and the doser corrects it.
  • Growth: each tier grows on a logistic curve driven by DLI, CO₂ and temperature.

Weather: a typical day near Pune for each season.

Season Outside Sun Summer (April) 22–38 °C, dry Clear Monsoon (July) 22–28 °C, humid Cloudy, with rain Winter (December) 12–30 °C Clear

docs.title: Three ways to run it
docs.text: Mode What it does Manual You set the vents, shade, fans, pad pump, fogging and irrigation in the polyhouse, and the lights, dimming, HVAC setpoint, CO₂ and dehumidifier in the vertical farm. Rules A typical controller. Thresholds with hysteresis: vents by temperature, shade above 650 W/m² or 30 °C, fan-and-pad above 30 °C until 27 °C, fogging below 55% RH. Irrigation on a timer, five 10-minute shots a day. Lights 06:00–22:00 at fixed setpoints. Only plain alarms. AI Model-predictive control, sensor-based irrigation, anomaly detection, vision, forecasts and the photoperiod optimiser, described below.

docs.title: Model-predictive climate control
docs.text:
Every 10 minutes the AI simulates 51 candidate plans one hour ahead, using the house model and the weather forecast. Each plan combines vents, shade, fans with or without the pad, and fogging.

Each plan gets a score in ₹-equivalent points: heat stress + VPD stress + leaf wetness + power and water − the crop value of the photosynthesis it allows. The lowest score wins.

The AI tab shows the chosen plan, the predicted temperature and VPD in an hour, and why it won. The explanation compares it with the best plan that changes only one setting.

docs.title: Sensor-based irrigation
docs.text: Each bed's valve opens on its own probe: when moisture falls near the bottom of the band, or after 0.5 MJ/m² of light since the bed's last pulse. That matches water to demand and to each bed.

docs.title: Anomaly detection
docs.text:
Inject a fault from the left panel and watch the AI find it. The Rules mode has plain alarms only.

Fault How the AI finds it What it does Pad pump failure Measured temperature is far above what the model expects with wet pads Closes the screen, re-plans without the pad, raises a maintenance alert Sensor drift on TH-3 The node disagrees with the other three by more than 1.5 °C after allowing for the pad-to-fan gradient Drops it from control (the Rules mode averages it in) Clogged drippers, bed 7 The bed dries faster, or needs its valve open far longer, than its neighbours Flags the bed for flushing Dosing pump B stuck Feed EC well above target Pauses dosing, flushes with clear water Gateway offline Uplink lost Edge controller falls back to local rules and buffers data HVAC compressor trip Room warming fast while cooling is demanded Dims the LEDs to 40% to cut heat NFT pump failure Rack return flow falls to zero Switches to the standby pump Rack fans failed Air speed sensor on the rack Schedules a repair; vision watches for tipburn LED driver failure PAR reads zero on a lit tier Raises a driver-swap ticket EC probe drift Probe disagrees with the dosing balance Recalibrates against the reference probe

docs.title: Plant-health vision
docs.text:
In the polyhouse a scouting robot drives every path. Cameras on its mast look at both rows, and a detector flags disease before it is obvious to the eye. Each find gets a spot spray over 2 m of the bed.

Without the AI, a worker scouts by eye at 09:00 each morning and finds only visible symptoms.

In the model's test the outbreak was found about 1.7 hours after onset and held to the 6 first plants. Under the rules it was found the next morning, after it had spread to 9 plants.

In the vertical farm a camera AGV photographs every tier for tipburn and wilting.

The detections are simulated; no image model runs in the browser.

docs.title: Photoperiod optimiser and forecasts
docs.text:
The vertical farm's lights run 16 hours a day for lettuce. The optimiser tries every start hour against the time-of-day tariff and the outdoor temperature (cooler night air raises the HVAC's COP). For a summer day it picks 22:00–14:00 instead of 06:00–22:00. In the 24-hour comparison that cuts the day's power and CO₂ cost by about 8%.

The AI tab also shows:

  • a polyhouse yield forecast from the climate index (photosynthesis against its light-limited potential) and disease losses;
  • a 7-day harvest forecast from each tier's growth curve.

docs.title: Rules against AI over 24 hours
docs.text:
The AI tab runs the same day twice on the model, once under the rules and once under the AI, with no faults.

For coloured capsicum in the polyhouse:

Season Hours over 3 °C too hot Photosynthesis vs potential Drip water Electricity Net value (crop value − running cost) Summer 9.0 → 1.6 59% → 79% 5,320 → 3,547 L 95 → 138 kWh ₹2,874 → ₹3,770 Monsoon 5.9 → 5.1 71% → 91% 5,320 → 2,376 L 3 → 45 kWh ₹3,218 → ₹3,840 Winter 1.4 → 0.0 60% → 98% 5,320 → 3,227 L 27 → 63 kWh ₹2,729 → ₹4,385

The AI spends more on fans and pad water when the crop value it protects is larger, and it uses less drip water.

In the monsoon it trades VPD for cooling at midday. The comparison shows that as well: VPD stays in band for less of the day than under the rules.

For lettuce in the vertical farm, the AI cuts the day's power and CO₂ cost by about 8% (₹8,327 → ₹7,620 in summer). It also keeps humidity in band most of the day, against about half the day under the rules, for the same growth.

docs.title: IoT network
docs.text:
Polyhouse node Measures TH-1 … TH-4 Air temperature and RH from the pad end to the fan end; CO₂ or PAR SM-1 … SM-12 Substrate moisture and temperature, one per bed FERT Feed EC, pH and flow PAD Pad pump current and sump level WS Outside temperature, RH, solar radiation and wind CAM The scouting robot's detections

The vertical farm has RK-1 … RK-4 (air, CO₂, PAR, air speed), NUT (EC, pH, DO, water temperature), FLOW-1 … FLOW-4, HVAC and CAM.

Every node reports every 5 minutes. The packets fly to the gateway in 3D, and the Dashboard lists each node's battery, signal and last report with a live MQTT feed (haritghar/ph/TH-2 {"t":26.8,"rh":68,"co2":412}). When the gateway goes offline, messages are buffered at the edge.

docs.title: PQC Road Works
docs.text:
A concrete road built step by step in 3D. The animation follows the construction sequence of a jointed plain concrete pavement (JPCP) with a pavement quality concrete (PQC) slab, as set out in IRC:15 (construction), IRC:58 (design) and MoRTH Specifications Section 600. It runs from the subgrade to opening the road to traffic.

Open PQC Road Works Source on GitHub

Note

Values shown are typical of IRC:15, IRC:58, IRC:57, IRC:SP:49 and MoRTH Sections 300–900. The contract specification and the current editions of the codes govern. The machines are generic.

docs.title: The road
docs.text: Item Value in the model Length 180 m, Ch 0+000 to 0+180 Carriageway 7.5 m (2 × 3.75 m), paved full width in one pass, with earthen shoulders Pavement 300 mm PQC (M40) · 150 mm DLC · 150 mm GSB / drainage layer · 500 mm subgrade Separation membrane 125 µm polythene between DLC and PQC Joints Transverse contraction joints every 4.5 m (39 joints); one longitudinal joint on the centre line Steel Dowels Ø38 × 500 mm @ 300 mm (25 per joint, 975 in all); tie bars Ø12 × 640 mm @ 600 mm (300)

docs.title: The ten stages
docs.text:
The timeline plays the stages in order. Click a stage in the list to jump to it, or drag the scrubber. Each stage has its own panel with:

  • what is done;
  • the requirements, with code references;
  • the plant and crew;
  • the quality checks.

A site clock shows the day and time.

# Stage Days What happens 1 Subgrade 1–4 Grader spreads, vibratory roller compacts the top 500 mm to ≥97% MDD 2 GSB / drainage layer 5–7 Tippers place aggregate, grader spreads, roller compacts 150 mm to ≥98% MDD 3 Dry lean concrete 8–15 DLC paver and tandem roller lay 150 mm; 7-day strength ≥10 MPa; cured 7 days 4 Separation membrane 16 125 µm polythene laid with ≥300 mm laps 5 Stringlines 16 Stakes at ≤5 m, tensioned lines for the paver's sensors 6 Slip-form paving 17, 06:00 Dumpers → placer-spreader → slip-form paver with DBI and TBI → texture-curing machine 7 Saw cutting 17–18 Transverse joints every 4.5 m within 4–24 h, ¼–⅓ depth; longitudinal joint ⅓ depth 8 Wet curing 17–31 Wet hessian for ≥14 days, water tanker, no traffic 9 Joint sealing 32–33 Groove widened, backer rod, sealant recessed 3–5 mm 10 Checks and opening 34–45 Shoulders, markings, 3 m straightedge, cores, beams; open at 28 days

docs.title: Slip-form paving
docs.text:
The paving train works as one unit, at about 1 m/min:

  1. Batching plant and dumpers: M40 paving concrete (design flexural strength 4.5 MPa) at ≤30 °C. Dumpers reverse in on the DLC and tip ahead of the spreader.
  2. Placer-spreader: spreads the concrete evenly in front of the paver.
  3. Slip-form paver: extrudes the full-width 300 mm slab between moving side forms.
    • An auger, internal vibrators, a tamper and the profile pan form the slab.
    • The oscillating correcting beam and super smoother finish the surface.
    • Its sensors follow the stringlines.
  4. Dowel-bar inserter (DBI): pushes 25 dowels into the fresh concrete at every joint position, at mid-depth.
  5. Tie-bar inserter (TBI): places tie bars along the centre line every 600 mm.
  6. Texture-curing machine:
    • Burlap drag first.
    • Then transverse tining: grooves ≈3 mm wide, 3 ± 1 mm deep, at random 10–21 mm spacing.
    • Then a spray of curing compound.

The HUD counts the slab length, concrete volume, dumper loads, dowels and tie bars.

X-ray steel makes the slab see-through, showing the dowels at each joint and the tie bars on the centre line:

docs.title: Joints
docs.text:
Two concrete saws cut the joints: - one goes across the road every 4.5 m; - the other runs along the centre line.

The HUD shows each joint's age when sawn against the 4–24 h window, and the QC log records it. After curing, the joints are widened, fitted with a backer rod and sealed.

docs.text:

  • Overview shows the whole stretch.
  • Section looks at the cut end of the pavement with each layer labelled.
  • X-ray steel and Labels can be switched on and off.

docs.text:
The drawings are generated for the chosen slab thickness (200–350 mm), with the dowel size picked from the IRC:58 table:

  • the transverse contraction joint: sealant, backer rod, initial saw cut, crack, and the dowel with its debonded half;
  • the longitudinal joint, with its tie bar;
  • a plan of two slab panels showing the joint layout.

docs.title: Calculator
docs.text:
For a chosen length, width, slab thickness, joint spacing, cement content, paver speed, haul distance and dumper size, the calculator gives:

  • volumes: PQC, DLC and GSB;
  • steel: contraction joints, dowels and tie bars, with their weights;
  • cement: tonnes and 50 kg bags;
  • logistics: concrete demand rate, dumpers needed, metres paved per day and days of paving.

docs.text: As the work passes, the log records: - field densities; - DLC cube results; - slump and concrete temperature; - beam sets; - dowel alignment; - joint sawing times and depths; - curing; - sealing; - straightedge, cores and 28-day flexural strength; - the opening date.

docs.title: Proto Lab
docs.text:
A 3D electronics bench for prototyping with Arduino, ESP32 and Raspberry Pi boards. You can:

  • place a board, a breadboard and sensors
  • wire them pin to pin
  • check the circuit for electrical mistakes
  • simulate it with live sensor values
  • copy the generated firmware

Open Proto Lab Source on GitHub

docs.title: Boards
docs.text:
Board Logic Highlights Code Arduino Uno R3 5 V ATmega328P, 6 PWM, 6 analog, SDA/SCL header Arduino C++ Arduino Nano 5 V Breadboard-friendly, 8 analog Arduino C++ Arduino Mega 2560 5 V 54 digital, 15 PWM, 16 analog, double header Arduino C++ ESP32 DevKitC 3.3 V Wi-Fi + Bluetooth, ADC1/ADC2, input-only and strapping pins Arduino C++ · MicroPython NodeMCU ESP8266 3.3 V Wi-Fi, single A0 input, D-pin names Arduino C++ · MicroPython Raspberry Pi Pico 3.3 V RP2040, 3 ADC, two I²C and SPI controllers MicroPython · Arduino C++ Raspberry Pi 5 3.3 V 40-pin header with BCM numbering, no ADC Python (gpiozero, Blinka) Raspberry Pi Zero 2 W 3.3 V 40-pin header, no ADC Python (gpiozero, Blinka)

Every header pin is modelled with its role (GPIO, 5 V, 3.3 V, GND, VIN) and its functions: PWM, ADC, I²C, SPI, UART, interrupts, DAC, ESP32 input-only, strapping and flash pins. Hover a pin to see them. The pins it connects to light up.

docs.title: Parts library (65)
docs.text:
• Environment: DHT11, DHT22, BME280, BMP280, SHT31, DS18B20, capacitive soil moisture, rain, MQ-2, MQ-135, water level.
  • Light & colour: LDR, BH1750, TCS34725, GUVA-S12SD UV.
  • Motion & position: HC-SR501 PIR, MPU-6050, ADXL345, Hall effect, tilt switch, rotary encoder, IR obstacle, line tracker.
  • Distance: HC-SR04, VL53L0X time-of-flight, Sharp IR.
  • Sound, touch & more: sound sensor, flame, TTP223 touch, MAX30102 pulse oximeter, HX711 load cell, INA219, ACS712.
  • Inputs: push button, potentiometer, joystick, RC522 RFID, IR receiver, NEO-6M GPS.
  • Outputs:
    • LED in six colours, RGB LED, active buzzer and passive piezo
    • SSD1306 OLED, 1602 I²C LCD, TM1637 7-segment display
    • MAX7219 8×8 matrix, 12-pixel NeoPixel ring
  • Motors & actuators: SG90 servo, relay module, DC motor + L298N, 28BYJ-48 stepper + ULN2003, bare DC motor.
  • Communication & storage: HC-05 Bluetooth, nRF24L01+, microSD, DS3231 RTC, ADS1115 ADC, 4-channel level shifter.
  • Breadboards & power: 830- and 400-point breadboards, MB102 breadboard supply, 9 V battery, 4 × AA pack.
  • Passives: resistors from 100 Ω to 100 kΩ, with colour bands.

Each part has a datasheet-style electrical profile:

  • supply range and typical current
  • I²C address
  • output level, and the minimum HIGH level its inputs need
  • 5 V tolerance of its inputs

docs.title: Building a circuit
docs.text:
• Place: click a part in the library. Drag parts on the cutting mat, and press R to rotate.
  • Breadboards: drop a part with header pins (a module, LED, resistor, button or breadboard-style board) onto a breadboard. It snaps into the holes and plugs in.
    • The a–e and f–j column strips and the four power rails connect it.
  • Wire: press W, click a pin or hole, then click another. Wires are coloured by convention: red for power, black for ground, and colours for signals.
  • Auto-wire: select a module and press ⚡ Auto-wire. Proto Lab picks the supply (3.3 V or 5 V, from the module's range and the board's logic level), GND, I²C/SPI pins, an analog pin for analog outputs, a PWM pin where one is needed, and free GPIO for the rest.
  • Inspect: the pin table shows every pin, its function, the hole it is plugged into and what it connects to.

docs.title: Circuit check
docs.text:
The Check tab builds a netlist from wires, breadboard strips and board-internal connections (all GND pins, Uno A4/SDA and A5/SCL). It then reports:

Check Example Shorts and mixed supplies 5 V wired to GND; 5 V and 3.3 V joined Supply range RC522 (3.3 V only) on 5 V; MQ-2 heater on 3.3 V Logic levels HC-SR04 ECHO (5 V) into an ESP32 or Raspberry Pi GPIO Pin functions analog sensor on a digital pin; I²C on non-I²C pins; TX→TX; Pi UART not on GPIO14/15; Pico SDA/SCL on different controllers Board quirks ESP32 input-only (34–39), strapping, flash and ADC2 pins; Arduino D0/D1 shared with USB; Pi HAT EEPROM pins LEDs missing series resistor, reversed LED, current from V, Vf and R I²C address clashes (MPU-6050 and DS3231 both at 0x68) Power budget current drawn from each 5 V / 3.3 V pin, MB102 or battery against its limit Grounds modules on an external supply without a common GND Motors DC motor straight on a GPIO pin; servos on the board's 5 V

Load Fault-finding challenge from the Examples menu for a circuit with five planted mistakes.

docs.title: Simulation
docs.text:
Press Simulate (or Space).

  • Sensors: each working sensor gets sliders or toggles in the Simulate tab. You can also click buttons, PIRs and touch pads on the bench.
  • Rules: rules such as when distance is below 20 cm → buzzer sounds drive the outputs. Outputs without a rule run a demo: LEDs blink, servos sweep, NeoPixels show a rainbow and motors spin.
  • What you see:
    • LEDs glow in their colour
    • servo horns turn, DC motor wheels and stepper shafts spin
    • the relay LED lights
    • OLED, LCD, 7-segment and LED-matrix displays show the latest readings
  • Serial monitor: prints the same line the generated firmware prints.

Only parts that pass the check and are wired to the main board take part, so a mis-wired sensor stays silent, as it would on a real bench.

docs.title: Generated code
docs.text:
The Code tab writes a complete starter program for the main board:

  • Arduino C++: for Uno, Nano, Mega, ESP32, ESP8266 and Pico (arduino-pico). Lists the Library Manager packages, for example Adafruit BME280, DHT, NeoPixel, SSD1306, LiquidCrystal I2C, ESP32Servo, TinyGPSPlus and RF24.
  • MicroPython: for Pico, ESP32 and ESP8266, using the built-in dht, onewire, neopixel and PWM modules plus common driver files.
  • Python: for the Raspberry Pi, using gpiozero for GPIO devices and Adafruit CircuitPython (Blinka) for I²C sensors and the ADS1115.

Each program follows the same structure:

  1. Set up the I²C, SPI and UART buses on the pins you wired.
  2. Read every sensor into a named variable, for example bme280_1_temp.
  3. Print the readings to serial.
  4. Apply your rules.
  5. Refresh the displays.
  6. Send CSV over Bluetooth, nRF24 or to the SD card when those parts are present.

A wiring comment at the top lists every connection.

docs.title: Robot Cell Studio
docs.text:
Design a factory robot joint by joint, see what it can reach and lift, then program it in a 3D work cell: palletizing, welding or driving screws. You can also teach your own moves. When the design works, export it as URDF.

Open Robot Cell Studio Source on GitHub

docs.title: Robots to start from
docs.text:
Preset Axes Typical use Rated payload* Reach 6-axis industrial arm 6 General handling, machine tending, welding ~7 kg 1.7 m 7-axis collaborative arm 7 Work next to people; the redundant elbow avoids obstacles ~11 kg 1.0 m SCARA 5 Fast, flat pick-and-place and assembly ~31 kg (quill) 0.7 m 5-axis palletizer 5 Stacking heavy cases and sacks ~83 kg 2.6 m Cartesian gantry 4 Accurate overhead handling over a rectangle ~125 kg 2.0 × 2.0 m

*Computed by the app from the motors you choose; see below.

docs.title: Building
docs.text:
A robot is a pedestal followed by a chain of joints, each with the link that follows it.

Joint Moves Example Yaw Turns about the vertical Waist of an arm, SCARA arms Pitch Bends about a horizontal axis Shoulder, elbow, wrist bend Roll Twists about its own link Forearm and wrist roll, cobot joints Slide Moves linearly along its link Gantry axes, SCARA quill

For every joint you can set:

  • the link direction (up, forward, sideways or down) and its length
  • the motor size: S 30 N·m, M 160 N·m, L 650 N·m, XL 2,200 N·m or XXL 7,500 N·m (or 400 N to 40,000 N for slides). Each size has its own mass, speed and cost.
  • the travel limits

You can add up to 9 joints, reorder them, change the pedestal height and colour, and fit a two-finger gripper, vacuum cup, MIG welding torch or screwdriver.

docs.title: Specs and checks
docs.text:
• Kinematics: forward kinematics are computed live for any chain. Horizontal reach and working height come from 1,400 random joint configurations, which can also be shown as a coloured workspace point cloud.
  • Rated payload: for 500 poses the app computes the static gravity load on every joint from link, motor and tool masses. The rated payload is the largest mass at the flange that keeps every motor under 85% of its rating in 95% of the workspace.
  • Joint load bars: show the live load on each motor against its rating, including the box being carried.
  • Warnings: an arm that cannot hold its own weight, payload under 1 kg, too few axes to orient the tool, parts of the arm through the floor, and unreachable program points.
  • Mass and cost: arm mass and an illustrative cost in ₹ lakh.

docs.title: Programming
docs.text:
• Task templates lay out the cell around your robot. They search conveyor, pallet and fixture positions and heights until every point of the program is reachable, with the tool pointing the way the task needs.
    • Palletize boxes: pick boxes from the end of a conveyor and stack 2 × 2 × 2 on a pallet (raised on a stand if the arm can't reach low). Shows boxes per hour.
    • Weld a seam: run a MIG torch around a rectangular seam. It uses a pushing angle if the arm can tilt the torch all the way round, otherwise vertical. Sparks, arc light and a growing weld bead are drawn.
    • Drive screws: fasten six screws into a plate.
    • Teach your own: an empty program.
  • Jog each joint with sliders, or switch to Drag TCP and move the tool with the handle. The arm follows with damped-least-squares inverse kinematics, solving position and tool-axis direction for any number of joints. Tool ↓ points the tool straight down.
  • Teach MoveJ (joint move) and MoveL (straight-line move) points, then add tool and wait steps.
  • Compile checks: each step is solved and checked for reach, straight-line feasibility (IK every 15 mm along the path), floor collisions and joint speed limits, then timed. Unreachable steps are marked and the cell's light tower turns red.

docs.title: Export
docs.text:
• URDF: links, revolute and prismatic joints with axes, origins, limits, effort and velocity, cylinders for visuals and collisions, and estimated masses and inertias. Ready for ROS 2, MoveIt, Gazebo or Isaac Sim.
  • Program script: a vendor-neutral .rcs listing of MOVEJ J[...], MOVEL P[...] AXIS[...], TOOL and WAIT lines, in degrees and millimetres.
  • Project: save or open JSON, or copy a share link that holds the robot design (#task=weld&r=…, or a preset such as #p=scara&task=palletize).

docs.title: Cartesian gantry
docs.text: Three linear axes on a portal frame plus a rotary wrist.

docs.title: 5-axis palletizer
docs.text: XXL shoulder motor and long links: 2.6 m reach, ~83 kg rated payload.

Engineering estimates

Payload, loads, masses and costs come from a simple static model. It covers gravity only, with no dynamics, deflection or safety factors beyond the 85% torque margin. Use it to compare designs and learn, not to size a real robot.

docs.title: गडकिल्ले · Forts of Swarajya
docs.text:
A 3D explorer of the forts of Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj in Maharashtra. Each fort stands on its real terrain, built from elevation data, with walls traced along the actual plateau edges and shorelines. A relief map of the Sahyadri and the Konkan coast connects them through a timeline of his life from 1630 to 1680.

Explore the forts Source on GitHub

docs.title: The forts
docs.text:
Fort Type Known for UNESCO 2025 शिवनेरी Shivneri Hill Birthplace of Shivaji Maharaj (19 Feb 1630) ✓ तोरणा Torna Hill Traditionally the first fort of Swarajya (c. 1646) राजगड Rajgad Hill First capital; Bale Killa with three machis ✓ सिंहगड Sinhagad Hill Tanaji Malusare's battle, 1670 पुरंदर Purandar Hill Birthplace of Sambhaji Maharaj (1657); Treaty of Purandar (1665) प्रतापगड Pratapgad Hill-forest Built 1656; Afzal Khan defeated 10 Nov 1659 ✓ रायगड Raigad Hill Capital; coronation 6 Jun 1674; passed away 3 Apr 1680 ✓ लोहगड Lohagad Hill Vinchu Kata spur above the Bor ghat ✓ पन्हाळा Panhala Hill-plateau Siege and escape to Vishalgad, July 1660 ✓ साल्हेर Salher Hill Highest fort in the Sahyadri; Battle of Salher, 1672 ✓ सिंधुदुर्ग Sindhudurg Island Sea fort begun 1664 off Malvan ✓ विजयदुर्ग Vijaydurg Coastal Triple walls; Maratha naval base ✓ सुवर्णदुर्ग Suvarnadurg Island The "Golden Fort" off Harnai ✓ खांदेरी Khanderi Island Fortified 1679 despite English and Siddi opposition ✓

The eleven Maharashtra forts marked ✓, together with Gingee in Tamil Nadu, form the Maratha Military Landscapes of India. These were inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in July 2025 at the 47th session of the World Heritage Committee.

docs.title: What you can do
docs.text:
• Map: a ×8 relief of real elevation from Salher in the north to Sindhudurg in the south, with the coastline and sea depth from the same data.
    • Saffron flags mark each fort, and you can click one to fly there.
    • Mumbai, Pune, Nashik, Kolhapur and Ratnagiri appear for reference.
    • No political boundaries are drawn.
  • Timeline: play through Shivaji Maharaj's life from 1630 to 1680. Each event highlights its fort and offers a 3D visit.
  • Fort view: about 3–4 km of real terrain at roughly 9 m resolution around each fort. It includes:
    • walls, bastions (buruj), battlements and gates
    • indicative buildings: temples, tanks, granaries, Raigad's throne court and samadhi, Pratapgad's equestrian statue, Khanderi's lighthouse
    • a waving saffron Bhagwa Dhwaj on the summit
    • Marathi and English labels
  • Seasons and light:
    • Monsoon: lush green with clouds drifting below the walls.
    • Winter: golden-green.
    • Summer: dry grass and fewer leaves.
    • The time-of-day slider moves the real sun for that fort's latitude and date.
  • Sea forts: animated sea with reflections around Sindhudurg, Vijaydurg, Suvarnadurg and Khanderi.
  • Tour: slow orbit; Labels on/off; deep links such as #/fort/raigad?season=monsoon&hour=7.

docs.title: Raigad in the monsoon
docs.text: The plateau rim traced from the cliffs, with the throne court, the samadhi, Takmak Tok and Hirkani Buruj.

docs.title: Rajgad
docs.text: Two rings: the Bale Killa citadel, and walls running down its three spurs (machis).

docs.title: Vijaydurg
docs.text: Triple walls on the headland at the mouth of the Waghotan creek.

docs.title: How the walls are traced
docs.text:
1. Elevation: terrain is baked from Terrarium elevation tiles (AWS Open Data, from Mapzen/Tilezen, based mainly on SRTM). The tiles are decoded in the browser as R·256 + G + B/256 − 32768 metres.
  2. Checking positions: each fort's position was checked against the data.
    • Hill forts sit on a local summit: Torna 1,399 m (published 1,403), Rajgad 1,360 m (1,376), Sinhagad 1,330 m (1,317) and Salher 1,566 m (1,567).
    • Island forts were re-centred on their islands.
  3. Hill forts: rays are cast from the summit until the ground falls a set depth below it, which follows the cliff line. Smoothing and resampling turn this into a wall line.
    • Forts with an upper citadel and lower spurs get two rings (Rajgad, Purandar, Pratapgad).
  4. Sea forts: rays start at the island's centre and stop at the sea. They tolerate up to about 90 m of low ground inside the island, but not the channel to the mainland.
  5. Placement: bastions are spaced every 55–85 m. Gates go where a ridge approaches the wall (the gentlest outward slope). Named places such as Takmak Tok are put at the steepest drop, and machis at the longest spurs.

Indicative, not surveyed

The terrain and wall lines come from real elevation data at about 30 m source resolution. Buildings and their positions are simplified illustrations, not archaeological plans. Historical notes are short summaries from public sources, and traditional or approximate dates are marked "c.".

docs.title: Solar System Explorer
docs.text:
A real-time 3D model of the Solar System, modelled on NASA's Eyes on the Solar System. Every planet sits where it really is today, at true scale, and you can fly from the whole system down to a single world, then speed time up or run it backwards.

Launch the explorer Source on GitHub

docs.title: What you can do
docs.text: Fly to any world Planet bar, search box (arrow keys + Enter), or click a label or sphere. The camera flies on a logarithmic path, so a trip from the Sun to Pluto takes a couple of seconds. Info card Radius, mass, sidereal day, orbital period, axial tilt, plus live distance from the Sun and Earth, light time and orbital speed. Show whole orbit frames the body's orbit; Close-up returns to it. Time controls −1 yr/s … real time … +1 yr/s, pause, and LIVE to jump back to now. Keyboard: Space pauses. Dates are limited to 1800–2050, the range of the orbital elements. Lighting Flood light lights every world evenly, like Eyes' lighting=flood. Turn it off for natural lighting: the Sun is the only light, so you see day, night and phases. Orbits & labels Toggle orbit lines (and the asteroid belt) and labels. Deep links #/<body>?lighting=flood\|natural&date=2030-01-01&rate=86400, e.g. #/saturn or #/earth?lighting=natural.

docs.title: Earth, natural lighting
docs.text: The globe is turned by Greenwich sidereal time and tilted to the real axis, so the day–night line matches the actual time.

docs.title: Saturn
docs.text: Rings from 74,500 to 140,220 km with a radial colour and transparency map, tilted 26.7° with the planet. Titan orbits in the ring plane.

docs.title: Jupiter
docs.text: Io, Europa, Ganymede and Callisto on their real distances and periods.

docs.title: How positions are computed
docs.text:
• Planets and Pluto: JPL's Approximate Positions of the Planets (E. M. Standish), Table 1 Keplerian elements and their century rates, J2000 ecliptic. Kepler's equation is solved with Newton iteration. Accurate to arc-minutes for the inner planets, a fraction of a degree for the outer ones, between 1800 and 2050.
  • Moon: a low-precision geocentric series from the Astronomical Almanac (≈ 0.3°). It is tidally locked, so the same face always points at Earth.
  • Other moons: the Galilean moons and Titan move on circular orbits with their real radius and period, in the parent's equatorial plane. Their phase is illustrative, not ephemeris-accurate.
  • Orbital speed: the vis-viva equation, v² = GM☉ (2/r − 1/a).
  • Asteroid belt: 4,000 illustrative particles between 2.2 and 3.3 AU, each moving at its Kepler rate on the GPU.

docs.title: Rendering at Solar-System scale
docs.text:
Everything is in kilometres at true size, from a 1,188 km Pluto to Neptune at 4.5 billion km. Two tricks keep it stable:

  1. Floating origin. Positions are kept in double precision in JavaScript. Each frame, the focused body is moved to the scene origin and everything else is placed relative to it, so the GPU never sees huge numbers near the camera.
  2. Logarithmic depth buffer. The camera's near plane is 1 km and its far plane is 2 × 10¹¹ km without z-fighting. Custom shaders (the asteroid belt) include three.js's logdepthbuf chunks.

Planets are too small to see from far away, so every body also has a fixed-size ring marker and an HTML label, as in Eyes.

docs.title: Turbofan Ops
docs.text:
Operate a high-bypass turbofan in 3D. You start it the way airline crews do, take it to take-off thrust, reverse it on landing and shut it down. While it runs you can see the air and hot gas move through a cutaway of the fan, compressors, combustor and turbines, and read the engine's state on cockpit-style gauges. You can also train on failures: a hot start, a stall, a bird strike, an engine fire.

Open Turbofan Ops Source on GitHub

docs.title: The engine
docs.text:
The engine is a generic two-spool, high-bypass turbofan of about 130 kN (29,000 lbf), the class that powers today's narrow-body airliners. Its numbers are illustrative and not those of any certified engine.

Module What it is Fan 18 swept, wide-chord composite blades with titanium leading edges; ≈ 1.98 m across, about 4,400 rpm Outlet guide vanes Straighten the bypass air Booster (LP compressor) 3 stages on the LP shaft HP compressor 10 stages on the HP spool, about 16,600 rpm Combustor Annular, 18 fuel nozzles, 2 igniters HP turbine 2 stages, drives the HP compressor LP turbine 7 stages, drives the fan and booster; EGT is measured here Thrust reverser Translating sleeve, blocker doors and cascade vanes Accessory gearbox Driven from the HP spool; carries the air turbine starter

Views:

  • Cutaway removes a quarter of the casings.
  • X-ray makes them transparent.
  • Exploded slides the modules apart.
  • Airflow shows particles through the inlet, bypass duct and core. They are blue in cold air and turn yellow, orange and red as the gas heats up through the compressor and combustor, then cool through the turbines.

The Learn tab explains each module and flies the camera to it.

docs.title: Starting the engine
docs.text:
The engine has a FADEC auto-start, as on modern airliners:

  1. APU BLEED ON: compressed air for the air turbine starter.
  2. ENG MODE → IGN/START, then ENG MASTER → ON.
  3. The FADEC opens the starter valve and N2 accelerates. At 16% N2 an igniter fires, and at 22% the fuel valve opens.
  4. Light-off should follow within 15 s. EGT rises to a peak of about 600 °C, and N1 starts to turn.
  5. At 50% N2 the starter cuts out and the igniters stop.
  6. The engine stabilises at idle: N1 ≈ 19.5%, N2 ≈ 58%, EGT ≈ 450 °C, fuel flow ≈ 300 kg/h. The whole start takes about 35 s.

A checklist in the cockpit tab ticks each step off as it happens.

docs.title: Flying it
docs.text:
The thrust lever has IDLE, CL, FLX/MCT and TOGA detents, and reverse below idle on the ground.

  • Take-off: N1 goes from idle to TOGA in about 7 s. The FADEC limits how fast fuel is added so the compressor does not stall. At sea level the engine makes about 120 kN with an overall pressure ratio of about 40, a bypass ratio of about 9 and EGT about 970 °C.
  • Hot days: the rating is flat up to ISA+15 °C. Beyond that the EGT limiter trims N1, and take-off thrust falls.
  • Cruise: select a flight condition up to cruise at FL350 / Mach 0.78. In cruise the engine makes about 15 kN at a TSFC of about 0.55 lb/lbf·h. In flight the spools keep windmilling with no fuel.
  • Landing: on the landing roll, pull the lever below idle. The sleeve slides aft, the blocker doors fold into the bypass duct and the cascades throw the fan air forwards. That gives about −27 kN of reverse thrust.

docs.title: Gauges and alerts
docs.text:
The cockpit tab has an EICAS-style display:

  • N1 and EGT dials with limits. N1 also shows a blue target marker.
  • Digital N2 and fuel flow.
  • Oil pressure, temperature and quantity, and vibration for both spools.
  • Status flags: starter valve, igniters, fuel, REV, AVAIL and FIRE.

Below it, ECAM-style messages give the warning or caution together with the procedure steps.

The Engine data tab shows:

  • temperature and pressure at each gas-path station (0, 2, 13, 25, 3, 4, 45 and 5)
  • performance: thrust, TSFC, airflow, bypass ratio, OPR, jet velocities, bypass share of thrust, propulsive efficiency and spool rpm
  • a 3-minute history of N1, N2, EGT and fuel flow

docs.title: Failures to practise
docs.text: Failure What happens What to do Hot start EGT passes the 725 °C start limit Auto start aborts and dry-cranks. In manual start, cut the master yourself Hung start N2 stops accelerating below idle Aborted after 60 s; retry No light-off Igniter A failed: no EGT rise within 15 s Abort, dry crank, retry on both igniters Compressor stall Bang, flames from inlet and exhaust, EGT spike, N1 drop The FADEC cuts fuel to recover; reduce thrust if it repeats Bird strike Damaged fan blade, high N1 vibration, a stall Reduce thrust to keep vibration down Engine fire FIRE warning, flames in the core compartment Idle, master off, pull the fire handle, agent 1, then agent 2 after 30 s Oil leak Quantity and pressure fall; bearings seize without oil Shut the engine down before it seizes Flameout Heavy rain puts the flame out at low power Select IGN or continuous ignition: the windmilling engine relights

docs.title: How the model works
docs.text:
• Spools: the core accelerates when fuel flow exceeds what it needs to hold its speed, plus starter torque during a start. The fan follows the core with a lag.
  • FADEC: the thrust lever sets an N1 target from the flight condition, with a flat rating. Fuel is metered within acceleration and deceleration schedules, an EGT limiter and overspeed limits. The FADEC also runs the start sequence and aborts.
  • Cycle: a quasi-steady Brayton cycle runs from the inlet through the fan, booster, HPC, combustor, HPT and LPT to the nozzles, using the ISA atmosphere and ram recovery. Turbine work balances compressor work, and thrust comes from the bypass and core jet velocities.

Everything runs in the browser with three.js and no build step. src/engine.js also runs in Node, where the start sequence, ratings and every fault were tested.

Note

Turbofan Ops is an illustrative training model of a generic engine. Its figures, limits and procedures are simplified and must not be used for real operations.

docs.title: यात्रा · Yatra: Rail & ST
docs.text:
Ride from Mumbai to Pune in 3D, either by Indian Railways through the Bhor Ghat tunnels and viaducts, or by MSRTC ST bus up the old Khandala Ghat road. On the way you pass stations and bus stands, signals and level crossings, and, in the monsoon, waterfalls. You can ride by day or by night.

Open Yatra Source on GitHub

docs.title: Two journeys
docs.text:
Railway Road Route Dadar → Thane → Kalyan Jn → Karjat → Khandala → Lonavala → Pune Jn Mumbai Central → Panvel → Khopoli → Lonavala → Pune (Swargate) Ghat Bhor Ghat, 1 in 37, 7 tunnels, 6 viaducts Khandala Ghat, hairpin curves, kerbs and crash barriers Climb Sea level to about 620 m Sea level to about 620 m Roadside Stations with platforms, canopies, foot over bridges and yellow name boards; colour-light signals; level crossings Bus stands with parked buses; milestones; painted roadside trees; oncoming trucks, cars and autos

The route is 40 km long, so a journey takes about 40 minutes at 1× and about 2 minutes at 20×. It keeps the real order of places and the climb from the Konkan up to the Deccan plateau, but compresses the distances in between.

docs.title: Trains
docs.text:
Train Top speed What you see Vande Bharat Express 130 km/h 8-car train set with aerodynamic driving cars. It runs non-stop through Karjat and Khandala. Express: WAP-7 + 18 LHB coaches 110 km/h Electric locomotive with pantograph, then general, sleeper, AC 3-tier, AC 2-tier, first AC and pantry coaches Mumbai suburban local 100 km/h 12-car EMU with open doors and people hanging on Freight: WAG-9 + 30 BCN wagons 75 km/h Covered wagons. It does not stop on the way.

Trains run on the left line of the double track, as in India. They are drawn on broad gauge (1,676 mm) under 25 kV overhead wires. Each coach follows the curves and gradients on its two bogies. Trains coming the other way pass on the right-hand line.

docs.title: ST buses
docs.text:
Bus Top speed Livery Lalpari (ordinary) 70 km/h Red with a yellow band and a roof carrier with luggage Hirkani (semi-luxury) 75 km/h Green and white Shivshahi (AC seater) 80 km/h White with an orange stripe and an LED destination board Shivneri (premium AC) 85 km/h White and blue, taller multi-axle coach e-Shivai (electric) 80 km/h White and green. It has no exhaust.

Buses keep left. At each stop they pull off the highway into the bus stand, wait, then rejoin traffic. Speeds on the ghat are limited by the curves, and the bus leans slightly into each turn.

docs.title: Driving
docs.text:
You don't need to drive: the driver accelerates up to each speed limit and brakes early for curves and stations.

  • Speed limits depend on the section (city, plains, ghat, plateau) and the curve radius.
  • Heavy trains slow on the 1 in 37 climb.
  • At each stop the vehicle halts for a dwell time, sounds its horn and leaves.
  • At the end of the route it arrives and, after a pause, starts again.

Signals show red behind the train, then yellow, then green, and show yellow ahead of a station stop. Level-crossing gates close as a train approaches and open after it passes.

docs.title: Cameras
docs.text:
Key Camera View 1 Chase Behind and above 2 Cab The driver's view 3 Side Alongside. At stations it stands on the platform. 4 Window From a seat, looking out at the valley 5 Line-side Standing beside the track as the train passes 6 Aerial From high up and ahead 7 Orbit Free camera

Other controls: Space pauses, H sounds the horn, 1×–20× changes the speed, and clicking the route strip jumps to any point. The strip shows the elevation profile, with tunnels drawn dark and bridges drawn blue.

docs.title: Weather, season and time
docs.text:
• Monsoon: rain, mist, low cloud, green hills and waterfalls on the ghat.
  • Winter: haze and dry grass.
  • Summer: clear skies and brown hills.

The time of day slider moves the sun. At night, carriage and bus windows light up and headlights come on. Headlights also come on in tunnels.

docs.title: Sound
docs.text:
Sound is off by default; turn it on with 🔊 or by pressing the horn. It plays:

  • the horn: a two-tone horn on the Vande Bharat, a three-tone horn on the other trains, and a bus horn
  • running noise, which gets louder in tunnels
  • the rail joints clicking under each bogie as the train passes over them

docs.title: Phone
docs.text: On a phone the panel moves below the view, and the playback controls stack on the right.

docs.title: Links
docs.text:
Open the app at a particular vehicle, camera, weather or point on the route:

#mode=rail&v=vb&cam=cab&w=monsoon
#mode=rail&v=express&cam=trackside&at=21000&w=winter
#mode=road&v=shivneri&cam=drone&at=22500
#mode=road&v=lalpari&cam=chase&hour=20

v is vb, express, local or freight for trains, and lalpari, hirkani, shivshahi, shivneri or eshivai for buses. at is metres along the route and hour is 0–24.

docs.title: How it is built
docs.text:
• src/route.js builds each route from sections with curvature and gradient. It works out the centreline, elevation, speed limits, and where the tunnels, bridges, stops and crossings are. It also generates the terrain: mountains on one side of the ghat, a valley on the other, and cuttings at tunnel mouths.
  • src/world.js creates the world in 300 m chunks ahead of the vehicle and removes them behind it. It builds:
  • the terrain
  • the track: ballast, rails, sleepers, overhead masts and wires, signals
  • the road: asphalt, kerbs, barriers, milestones
  • tunnels, viaducts, stations, bus stands, level crossings, waterfalls, people and scenery
  • src/vehicles.js models the trains and buses. Liveries are drawn on canvas textures.
  • src/main.js holds the driving logic, other traffic, signals, sky and weather, cameras, HUD and sound.

It uses plain three.js with no build step.

Note

Yatra is a fan-made illustration. Liveries and rolling stock are approximations, and the project is not affiliated with Indian Railways or MSRTC. Distances are compressed and the scenery is generated. It is not a survey of the real line or road.
